utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Maisonneuve.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic, sometime in the course of this session, and hopefully before you finish your cross-examination, we'll give you a decision on the objections that were taken yesterday to this evidence. There are certain passages, specific passages, involved and I want to be precise in what I'm telling you. So somebody's working on typing up my manuscript and I will give you that hopefully before you finish your cross-examination. But meanwhile, please just continue with the questions from yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Crosland -- [In English] I do apologise because Colonel Crosland was in my mind about some issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The day can only get better, Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Good morning, General Maisonneuve.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will pick up from where I left it yesterday, MM/14, which deals with the meeting taking place on the 23rd of January, 1999, where in addition to Drini, Mr. Smith, Lefever, and another person were present. In item 2 of the annexed document there is the detailed description of an ambush at Bela Crkva where KLA members were involved. The vehicle containing KLA members seemed to have been caught by accident. I would like you to tell me if you were aware of the fact that Bela Crkva was one of the strongholds of the KLA.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] I knew that there was a presence -- a KLA presence in Bela Crkva.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You also know, I suppose, a member of your mission, Mr. Frank Letvic?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: He was there on the spot and he learnt all this. I suppose he reported to you on what had happened on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if it's possible to get the read-out here, but I don't recall exactly the Bela Crkva incident that you're speaking about. And if I could have a look at the actual notes, that would help me refresh my memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: In the documents received from Prosecution, we don't have a report by Mr. Letvic. We only know what I told you, a general report from the meeting. I would merely want you to confirm the identity of your verifier and that is enough for me at this time. Thank you. My learned friend Sepenuk, whom we address as General, referred to this same document and mentioned a threat to urban terrorism. I would like to know whether you knew whether these threats in fact materialised where explosive devices were set at Podujevo, Urosevac, it Mitrovica, and such-like places. On these occasions there were several wounded and as many as nine persons were killed. I will just remind you of Mitrovica on the 13th of March, 1999, a bomb at the market there, several wounded and dead. You received that sort of information, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember specifically the Mitrovica incident to which you refer, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General, sir. From the same set of documents, MM/14, there's minutes from a visit to a house in Drina on the 28th of January. There were you, Drini, and Mike Morwood --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't catch the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: -- in the same minutes discussion was carried out about the possible setting up of an office in the village of Planeja next to the border. On this occasion Drini said, and this is the last paragraph: "I'm not sure if I'm aware of what the final deadline for leaving or vacating the village is." Can you explain to us what this is all about. Who issued a deadline for the village to be vacated?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well on several occasions the KLA in particular, but also the authority forces in -- in Kosovo, tried to set deadlines that they wanted us to adhere to. And we made the point repeatedly to them that we did not do deadlines, i.e., that the OSCE was not working on any deadlines from the parties in the theatre.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Marcussen is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I was just going to seek clarification of what part of this document my learned friend was quoting from. Is it the first --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The last paragraph, he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Yes, but that doesn't talk about the deadline of 15 minutes. That's another bullet point. One, two, three, four, five, six. It's the sixth bullet point and I don't think that talks about vacating a village, so I was just confused about what it actually is. I think it's a deadline for the KVM to evacuate a certain point before what might be an attack. But it might be that I'm misunderstanding. That's what I'm seeking the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Where is the reference, Mr. Cepic?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: If you give me just a minute, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If you go, Mr. Marcussen --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- to the -- if you go to the last page of that which is headed "Record of Discussions," and D final paragraph: "Unknown but Aware of Deadlines to Leave Village." This is on sheet 5717.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Sorry. I thought we were at the last of those attachments to the document. Sorry. That's my mistake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This is MM/14.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: But there are a number of -- there are three or four documents in that and we were -- just before we were at the last one of the documents that's attached under that tab. But --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, this is the last one I have under MM/14, so you're maybe in a different order from me. The next one is 14A in my bundle.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I may be even more confused, then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Mr. Cepic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I suppose you're aware, General, that many Albanian villages in the border area were given an order by the KLA to move out, specifically on the eve of Strela Operation which was supposed to be launched from Albania in the direction of Djakovica and Prizren?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is there a date for that, Mr. Cepic?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Some of the evidence relating to the period concerning Strela Operation I used in my cross-examination of Mr. Zyrapi. This is the beginning of April already, at the time when General Maisonneuve was not in Kosovo, but there was mention of the population moving out from Albanian itself, and I wanted to know whether General knew anything about it, since he was present in Albania at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you have the answer so please --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- move on to something he's likely to know about, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: General, we heard a lot about disproportionate use of force yesterday. In paragraph 18 of your statement you say that in principle, the responses by the army and the police, when these are provoked or when they are thought to be provoked, were disproportionate to the provocation involved, and this is stated in paragraph 18 of your statement.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [In English] Thank you. [Interpretation] You will agree with me that the activities by the KLA in Kosovo oftentimes had the character of sabotage actions, ambushes. As you described yesterday the incident on the 8th of January had the character of rebel actions, trench-type combat, attacks against buildings and facilities. Isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Yesterday in the course of your evidence when answering the questions by the Prosecutor, transcript page 51, line 11, stated that in the fighting against rebel terrorist forces, special or lightly armed units were engaged. If there were no such special units and in view of the widespread activity of the rebel forces, am I right in saying that conventional forces should be used instead, such as the Rules of Engagement FM3 of the US item 9-37 which states: "Terrorist attacks oftentimes have disproportionate effects, even against conventional forces." Rule 9-38: "The commander engaging conventional forces against organised terrorist forces active within his area of responsibility shall carry out conventional offensive attacks and not anti-terrorist activities."

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of the US rules of engagement to which you refer; however, I guess as a rule, as a military person, I would certainly use the means at my disposal to react to attacks if the terrorists can be identified and if there's a possibility of retaliation. But also as a military officer I would say that you tend -- I would certainly direct my troops to reply in a proportionate fashion, no matter what the rules of engagement say.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, I'd like to hear your opinion in view of what was said before. The situation is as follows. The adversary is well entrenched, well-fortified. How can the enemy be neutralised if they are fortified in an area such as Dulje Stibe [phoen] where they were well-entrenched or if they are well-fortified in buildings and from there opening fire upon your units. And the area in front of these facilities is laid with mines; therefore, you can't have infantry forces advance into the area, is in such situations the use of armoured units at half a distance justified in order to neutralise the attack against one's own forces?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in the scenario you describe, there's no question that that would be the proper employment of armoured forces, but that is not a type of scenario that I ever saw in terms of a dug-in enemy. What I saw was mostly hit-and-run tactics that were -- of course they would be hidden, for example, in this particular ambush of the 8th of January, there's no question --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now that you've mentioned ambushes, let us clarify one thing. As we said -- mentioned several times, the situation on the 18th [as interpreted] of January, 1999, where you state that later on from a combat position at Dulje a tank appeared, firing rounds at the village of Slapuzane. This was in the case against Milosevic transcript --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't catch the page --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: -- you said yesterday --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We need the page. Mr. Cepic, you're going a bit quickly for the interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Transcript page 5784 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: -- line 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You said that there was one tank. Yesterday on page 61 of your evidence you stated that several tanks were active.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the meantime could the court officer pull up P733, please, on to the screens.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could you confirm the date, please, Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 8th of January, 1999, three police officers were killed. Later on you described the situation, and as I said, in the Milosevic case you mentioned one tank, whereas yesterday's, you mentioned that there were several tanks. This isn't the most important issue now. The most important thing is the following one. I went carefully through your reports for that day --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let's take them one at a time. Can we clarify this because --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm afraid, Your Honour, I can't remember if there was one tank or many tanks. All I remember is my people reporting that at least one tank was firing into the city and into the town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: How's your memory of these events today compared with 2002 when you gave evidence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's not as good as it was then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thanks. Mr. Cepic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could the court deputy play P733, please. I don't have it on my screen. [In English] Next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, we have one of the Prosecution exhibits in front of us and this is a report by your mission talking of this very same incident. There, the KLA action is being condemned as well as the kidnapping of soldiers at a different location. What I would like to point out is that this document doesn't state anywhere that any sort of force was employed by the Yugoslav Army; quite the contrary, it is stated that the response was quite restrained. Do you allow for the possibility that you received inaccurate information from the field, at least in part?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly not in terms of the tank firing into the town, because indeed I spoke to the individual -- the verifier who actually spoke to the tank commander and told him to stop. And indeed he followed that direction. The firing stopped. And I subsequently went into the village myself to check on the damage and to speak to the people in the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the meantime could Prosecution Exhibit P638 be prepared.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I just wanted to ask if we had been notified about those particular documents. I only remember seeing some videos yesterday being given to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really can't recall. At any rate, this is a Prosecution document that has been used so far.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We have an accord, don't we, for notifying the Prosecution of the documents you're likely to use so that they can prepare themselves in view of the mass of material. It sounds as though you didn't do that here, Mr. Cepic, but it's something to bear in mind each day. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I understood. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I suppose that your verifier informed some of the commanding officers in the army. Do you know that on the basis of this piece of information about allegedly one tank round having been fired, the 3rd Army of the VJ conducted an investigation in order to ascertain whether fire was indeed opened, that the military centre in Pristina was informed accordingly as well as the communications administration of the Yugoslav Army General Staff, and the result or the outcome of the investigation was that none of the rounds were fired. And this was the upshot of an extensive investigation. At any rate, you received this information from the army?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not remember receiving that information, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Have you got the communication, Mr. Cepic, to let the general see it?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, not now. I haven't got that document in the system, but it will be prepared probably for Defence case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Paragraph 18 of your statement is where you say that in most of the cases it seemed that the police and the VJ acted independently, each under their own command, although there was a high degree of cooperation and coordination in some actions. Now I would like to refer to one of the rules of the land army of the US, item 445, and the rule states that: "Within the area of anti-terrorist operations, in the absence of command authority, the commanders shall cooperate and achieve a consensus in order to achieve a unified action." Do you agree with me that cooperation and coordination between police and military forces is essential when dealing with anti-terrorist activities?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. Yes, I do agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. You received a lot of information in your regional centre. I'd like to know whether you received the information concerning the existence of military camps for the training of KLA members in the territory of the state of Albania along the border belt opposite Prizren, where KLA members underwent training under -- and held by foreign trainers and they would be infiltrated into Kosovo along the -- across the Pastrik mount. Did you have any information to that effect?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have specific information, but, of course, it was always talked about that there were rumours and there were allegations that these camps existed. I did not in fact -- when I went into Albania after, I didn't get a chance to visit or confirm or deny these allegations.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: General, I suppose you're aware of the fact that in a number of villages of the areas of Prizren, Suva Reka that were within the area of your regional centre, at the end of 1998 great amounts of weapons were being returned that the KLA had previously distributed to the villagers, and more than a 50 villages were involved in this?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall specifically that that was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that the verifiers of your mission oftentimes went to the villages occupied by the Albanians and spoke to the villagers concerning the stability, villages Orcusa, Zub-Damjane, Zub-Vrbnica, these are the villages among others.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: My verifiers tried to be very active and speak to both parties and of all ethnic backgrounds in my area.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. One of your verifiers was Mr. Trevor Wilson, was he not, from Great Britain?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly. The name -- that name doesn't ring a bell. David Wilson does, but not Trevor.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Then we will not go into that any further. Is it correct, General, that you were at the head of one of the teams of your mission which visited all three combat groups of the Army of Yugoslav from the Pristina Corps which were at [indiscernible] and Lapusnik and had no comments to make on the 24th of January, 1999?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed I did visit those locations with the authorities, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The real question was you had no comments to make. What's the answer to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In fact, the combat teams were deployed in accordance with the agreement. Those were agreed locations and we had freedom of movement to go visit those with -- accompanied by VJ commanders. In fact, Colonel Kotur was with me, I believe, at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday there was mention about entering the border belt. You know that entry into the border belt had to be announced in advance through the liaison officer because of the possibility of ambushes which happened frequently and for the sake of putting in place security measures. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the approach that we took was to request through the liaison officer an accompanying officer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That again wasn't the question. I think -- I think you were critical of the arrangements for visiting at the border belt, and Mr. Cepic's question is designed to say that there was justification for that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- because of the possibility of ambushes and for the sake of putting in place security measures. Now, what's your comment on that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, my comment would be that there's no question that there would have been possibilities of ambush anywhere in Kosovo, but my sense was that the KVM was there to -- in fact, to verify the situation and always travelled of course in orange vehicles. And I would think that the security of the verifiers along the border area, the border belt as it's described, would have been just as great as it was in the rest of Kosovo. So I didn't understand the -- in fact, I believe that the reasons given were not in accordance with the mission of the KVM.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, did you have information that the Army of Yugoslavia, or rather, its units in your area of responsibility were not authorised by the higher levels outside of Kosovo to permit visits to the border area that were not previously announced through the liaison officer? Did you have such information through Colonel Delic?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: And you are aware that any army, including the Army of Yugoslavia, has a very strict hierarchy?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I also believe you are aware that a joint procedure was put in place by the Kosovo Verification Mission and the Army of Yugoslavia for entry into these restricted areas. Colonel Ciaglinski said something about this. Did you know that this procedure was being prepared?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would also like to ask you the following. You know that your verifiers attended or were present at numerous military activities, such as target practice and combat to secure the border ceremonies, joint exercises for the procedure to be employed when members of the mission were there. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a good -- a good level of cooperation between my verifiers and the VJ.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Did you have the impression that the Army of Yugoslavia was concerned about the security of your mission?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would now like to go back to the village of Planeja. Would I be correct in saying that quite often you would get erroneous information and your patrols would go on the spot and would then establish that the situation was quite different? An example of this would be the village of Planeja, where information was received that on the 20th of January the village was shelled and looted, but your verifiers, as reported in the report of your regional centre on daily activities for the 29th of January, 1999, a patrol of your regional centre visited the village and found that life was going on as normal, that there have been no injuries -- or rather, no violations according to what I said before?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think in general terms it would quite often happen that we would get information that was of such a precise nature that by the time we would send a patrol, it wasn't -- we weren't able to confirm it. At times, of course, it was out of proportion, i.e., they would embellish what happened. So that did happen on occasion. In the specific case of Planeja on the 29th of January, if it was reported in the minutes or in the daily incident report, I'm sure that it's exactly what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Just a few more questions. Now I'm interested in the following. In your statement and in your testimony in the Milosevic case, there was mention of the fusing of KDOM into the Kosovo Verification Mission. Would it be correct if I said that members of the US KDOM and the European KDOM were not fully fused with the KVM all the time until the 20th of March, 1999, when the mission left Kosovo, that they actually acted independently of the Kosovo Verification Mission?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that would be a correct statement. In my case I had members -- some members of the US KDOM integrated into my command, but I think others stayed out; you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Did you receive a report from US KDOM that in the course of the autumn 1998 they had carried out verification of the weapons in the Pristina Corps and that everything had been done successfully. Did you receive such a report?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Yesterday on page 69 of the transcript, there was mention of Messrs. Delic and Loncar. During your testimony you pointed out more than once that the VJ was a professional army and that Delic and his soldiers acted only on orders. You also stated the same in your testimony and in paragraph 25 of your statement as well as page 69 of the transcript, where Delic said, "Loncar is not my commander, he's a liaison officer." In your army was there a procedure put in place?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the liaison officers, Mr. Cepic?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. Just let me finish my question, because the point is something else. Is there a procedure in place in your army and other armies, especially armies of NATO, that officers cannot decide on their own on activities in their area and that they cannot take orders from outside the chain of command or from civilian authorities, even if the civilian authorities are at the highest state level, that the chain of command, in other words, has to remain intact?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say that that -- that that is not always an absolute and -- for the most part, I think generally, you're right, that the chain of command of course must stay inviolate , and the reason why I'm kind of hedging here is because there are times when, of course, officers are provided or receive, if you wish, appropriate delegation of authority from the chain of command to be able to make decisions or to coordinate in certain areas. Is that clear?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: But the chain of command was inviolate in this particular case as it has to be in general in every army. That was my question.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say that's a general statement that applies, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Carry on. I would like to hear the next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: In this particular case the chain of command remained intact, it remained inviolate, I'm referring to the situation you described regarding Delic and Loncar. For the record, please, could you --

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think that is the case and I think that's what Colonel Delic was telling me was that General Loncar did not have authority to be able to make this kind of decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [In English] Thank you very much, General Maisonneuve.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I haven't got any further questions. I just finished in English because you started in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yesterday on this same topic I had the impression that you thought that Loncar should fit somewhere into the chain of command.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My sense, Your Honour, is that I would have thought that because General Loncar -- and again, this is perhaps a misperception on my part at the time, that he had been given delegated authority to coordinate the work or the -- the activities of the VJ in the Kosovo theatre. And therefore, I would have thought that he, through the chain of command which -- through the corps commander, presumably, would have been able to actually make decisions or ensure that indeed permission was given in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That was the first time, I have to say, I had the impression that he might be part of a chain of command. Up until now I've been under the impression that a liaison officer was a go-between and didn't have command responsibilities and indeed had been brought into the set-up in -- I think in a couple of cases out of retirement to fill a particular sort of -- I don't know if it's almost a role of a mediator but it's certainly a liaison role.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we sometimes called it certainly in my army a coordination role. If he's the same rank as the corps commander, obviously wouldn't come in and take over the corps, but he would be charged - and this would be in my army and I think a professional army - would be charged with direction from the actual chain of command, let's say in this case Belgrade, perhaps, to pass the information on -- coordinate with KVM and then pass the information on to the corps commander so that the decisions could be made appropriately. So it depends how much authority he was delegated and what his terms of reference actually were, I think, in the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But Delic was telling you, "Although I'm a colonel, it's my word that goes here and not that of Loncar"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, Delic was -- what he was telling me was that Loncar's role was only as a liaison officer, that he could not give Delic direct orders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'd like now to deal with the objections that were stated yesterday to passages of this evidence and give you the Trial Chamber's ruling on it. There was a Defence motion in writing which we received only after we had come on to the bench requesting us to exclude portions of the evidence of the witness. We also heard oral submissions on the matter from both parties. I made a tentative ruling to give some guidance for cross-examination at that stage and indicated that the position would be more formally determined overnight and that a decision would be given to you today. And the Chamber now makes its ruling on the admission of the evidence of the witness. Dealing, first of all, with the statement. The statement of the witness will be admitted except for paragraph 34. Dealing now with the transcript from the Milosevic case, that will be admitted minus the following sections which will not be admitted: Page 5768, lines 8 to 10; 5787, lines 9 to 18; 5795, line 8 to 5796, line 23; 5797, lines 14 to 25; 5800, line 8, to 58 -- sorry, to 5805, line 14; 5840, line 22, to 5848, line 11; 5849, line 8, to 5853, line 16; 5855, line 15 to 5892, line 5; and 5903, line 23, to 5909, line 19. As far as the exhibits are concerned, the decisions that I give are confined to the ones to which exception was taken, and that was set out in paragraph 4(B) of the motion to exclude testimony. MM/7 will not be admitted; MM/8 will be admitted; MM/13 will not be admitted; MM/13A will be admitted, except for the assessment section on page 2, which will not be admitted; and MM/13B will not be admitted. In relation to MM/15 and 16, the Chamber accepts the Defence argument that these documents are substantially similar to As Seen, As Told and Under Orders which the Chambers deemed to be legally admissible but nevertheless denied admission into evidence in the exercise of its discretion pursuant to Rule 89(C) on the basis that the Prosecution had failed to show that they bore sufficient indicia of reliability in order to be admitted as hearsay evidence. That decision was issued on the 1st of September, 2006. So for similar reasons, the Chamber, having considered these documents, hereby denies their admission into evidence. I want to say something about the reasoning behind this decision. As set forth in the decision on the application of Rule 73 bis on the -- issued on the 12th of July, the Chamber has removed the charges in relation to Racak from the indictment and will not be rendering verdicts upon the alleged killings there in the final judgement. The parties should, therefore, tailor their adducement of evidence to issues other than those going to the specific alleged killings in Racak on the 15th of January, 1999. Issues that are potentially relevant to the indictment in relation to Racak may include the following: Coordination between the VJ and MUP in the vicinity of Racak in January 1999, command and control of the VJ and MUP in the same area at the same time, the activities of the OSCE-KVM at the same place and same time, and the disproportionate use of force in that area in January 1999, and in relation to that issue, also the presence and strength of KLA forces in the vicinity of Racak in January 1999. In other words, the parties are hopefully being directed by the Chamber to the territory that is relevant and ought to be explored and hopefully guided and advised by the Chamber not to expend significant resources upon the litigation of who may or may not have been killed at Racak on the 15th of January, 1999. If the parties choose to adduce further evidence in relation to Racak, it should be tailored as narrowly as possible to the issues described above. Now, in light of this, because we have picked our way through the transcript, in particular, it may be that there are passages to which objection was taken which the Defence might wish restored for the sake of balance. We've had that in mind in going through it in detail, and we think we've reflected the position fairly. There may be passages that you can instantly identify which we've excluded and which look as though they're favourable to the Defence, but it might be a speech to which there's no specific answer. So we've tried to tailor it to reflect the position fairly. But we will consider an application to restore any passages wrongly excluded in the view of the Defence if that is the case. Now, in light of that, Mr. Cepic, do you have any further cross-examination for Mr. Maisonneuve?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, by your leave, may I go through the transcript during the cross-examination of Mr. Ivetic once more. I believe I will not have any more questions, but I would like to check.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: After we've heard any further cross-examination from other counsel, then I will give you an opportunity if you wish. You must tell me, though, if you wish another opportunity to cross-examine at that stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is he the only other Defence counsel with questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a few questions, very few.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Who's going first? Mr. Ivetic or Mr. Fila?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, good day. My name is Toma Fila. I appear for Nikola Sainovic. In paragraph 9 of your statement and during yesterday's testimony on page 36, lines 1 to 5, you said that you met Sainovic once and that you attended that meeting with Ambassador Keller who chaired the meeting. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: It was a brief meeting, less than an hour. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: From my recollection, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And everybody spoke, not just Sainovic; right?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And based on that brief meeting you said that it was your impression that he was well-informed, polite, and that he was authorised to act. That's something we will be dealing with. You also said that in response to a question by the Prosecutor on page 36, lines 16 to 20, and you said you don't remember him having the need to consult anyone during the meeting. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, that's correct. I was trying to get a sense of the -- an impression of the man.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, are you aware that as a consequence of the Milosevic-Holbrooke Agreement, which none of us have seen yet but apparently it exists, by a decision of the Government of Yugoslavia signed by its president, Momir Bulatovic, Nikola Sainovic was appointed president of the Federal Commission for Cooperation with the OSCE, that is, with you also. And that in Article 2 of that document - as you know, it's a Defence document, 2108. I've shown it so many times that everybody knows it off by heart now. And it says there that he has to be well-informed, that he has to monitor the situation, and that he has to look after your security. That's the commission, not he personally. And that was on the 16th. And it was signed by the minister of foreign affairs, minister of interior, and so on, and General Loncar was another member of that commission. Are you aware of the existence of that body and that Nikola Sainovic was its chairperson?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in detail, but I am aware that Mr. Sainovic had been delegated responsibility to coordinate the Kosovo theatre.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I wanted to ask you the following. Does this explain your impression of his powers, the position he held?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Undoubtedly, yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, as an officer you fight with ammunition, and we fight with words and words can sometimes kill worse than bullets. That's why I'm putting these questions, not because I enjoy putting them, but because I have to. The Prosecutor wanted to hair something else, of course. I assume that you know that this was not the first meeting chaired by Keller, where he met Sainovic, that they had more than one contact? I'm referring to Mr. Keller and Mr. Sainovic.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would imagine he did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I also assume that -- and I hope that Ambassador Keller was more privy to the powers held by Sainovic than you are --

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure he was, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Will you, therefore, agree with me that in -- keeping in mind the knowledge Ambassador Keller had as the chairman of the meeting, that both of them knew what their respective powers were and that the meeting -- and that during these meetings Sainovic did not have any need to consult with anyone. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I thank you. I would like to ask you something out of the context, out of curiosity. At one point yesterday you said that you met two Albanians and that they were some sort of your own personal security, they were refugees. Can you tell us in what sense were they providing security for you. And when you give me this answer, can you tell me did others have Albanians as their security guards; and if so, were these Albanians armed? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they were not armed. They were local personnel employed to do physical security of our buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I apologise that I sat down. It was a discourtesy to you. Please go on.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they were not armed. They were physical security officers that would patrol, you know, around our headquarters, more for physical security purposes than for any kind of armed attack. It was for, you know, to keep people from stealing, et cetera, and to -- they were this kind of security folks. Locally employed civilians is what we were using for that purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I've finished. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good day, General. My name is Dan Ivetic and I represent Sreten Lukic and I have a series of questions for you today and I ask you to pay close attention to my questions so we can try and get through them with the most accurate and truthful answers possible. Since we do speak the same language I've been asked by the interpreters to remind myself and yourself that we do need to pause in between each of our respective comments or statements so they can accurately keep up with us, and I'll try my best and hopefully we'll get through it. First of all, sir, we've heard about your military career prior to being second into the OSCE verifier mission in Kosovo and Metohija. Am I correct that your professionally career does not include any experience working as a civilian police officer in any capacity?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. And furthermore, am I correct that you have not had any police-specific formal training or post-secondary education?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And as part of your training for the OSCE-KVM mission insofar as you were not intended to be a police verifier, you did not receive any additional or extensive police-specific training as part of the preparations for your deployment, did you?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, there were other persons within the OSCE-KVM that were dedicated police observers and verifiers. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you know what percentage of the KVM police verifiers had any prior training or experience as law enforcement or police officers?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could not put a percentage on them, but I had several of them in my -- in my particular regional centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm waiting for the transcript to catch up with us. Now, if you could turn for a moment to the agreements that you were tasked with verifying -- and these are the agreements reached around October 1998. As far as these agreements are concerned, am I correct that they were all negotiated prior to the arrival of yourself and the KVM, primarily by the US KDOM and others involved in the negotiation process?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And as far as the agreement as to the number of police or MUP personnel that were to be permitted in Kosovo, am I correct that the base-line figure that was established, that is to say the number of MUP personnel allowed in Kosovo was roughly 10.000 and some odd persons?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's -- I must tell you that I don't recall the exact number that had been negotiated or agreed upon, but that's a number I've heard on several occasions before.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: In any event, there was a fixed number that --

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe there was a fixed number.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Fair enough. And do you recall if this fixed number had been reached by KDOM, by the US KDOM as part of the negotiation process with the Serbian authorities, and if that number had been communicated to the KVM?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I believe it had and it would make sense that it would have been.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Fair enough, sir. Now, based upon the information that you obtained or that the KVM obtained after implementation of the agreements, the Serbian MUP abided by this agreement and reduced their personnel levels in Kosovo. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I can tell you is that while I was on the ground, personally I did not see any instances of reinforcement of the -- of the MUP presence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: From outside of Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, with respect to the KVM monitors, am I correct that there were some -- you've mentioned about reports that came in that were sometimes exaggerated or compounded upon. But with respect to the monitors, did you experience a problem with certain monitors that were either inexperienced or were relying primarily on second-hand information rather than going out into the field to verify things?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say there were a minimum of those types of instances. We really tried to -- in fact, that was part of the training that we gave the verifiers and it was part of the -- kind of the daily interaction we had with them to ensure that they would not become emotionally involved and therefore embellish situations.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now if we can just move briefly to Racak and I'm going to try and keep my questions tailored to the guide-lines that the Trial Chamber specified. Now, first, with respect to the activities of the KVM. Prior to undertaking the operation at Racak to arrest and disband members of the KLA that had been involved in attacks or killings in the area, it is presented that the local police officials in Stimlje and Urosevac not only gave notice of their operation that they were going to undertake to arrest individuals in Racak but engaged in lengthy discussions with the local KVM personnel, including a David Meyer, regarding the same. Do you have any knowledge of that?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not, but I'm not surprised, because in fact, as you know, it was outside my area; and if those negotiations had been taking place, it would have been with Regional Centre 5 which was covering that area at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: So you would have to defer to anyone who was actually involved in that process?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If such notification and discussions were underway, that would be in compliance with the agreement that the KVM was verifying. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The aspect -- I guess, the aspect of ensuring that coordination would take place and that it would be done in -- accompanied by verifiers, international observers, I think would have been in accordance with the agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. We have had some evidence in this case, in particular we have an exhibit that was referred to in your discussions with my colleague Mr. Sepenuk from Warrant Officer Christopher Clark, one of the verifiers on the ground who talked about the notifications that took place and the notification that came before Racak. He also specified that the KVM plan was to place various verifier vehicles on the scene to watch what was going on and that these orders were issued but that two KVM vehicles did not leave the Stimlje police station, basically disobeying their instructions. Do you have any knowledge of that?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Maisonneuve, remind me how it was you came to be involved in Racak at all, since it was outwith your area.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it was on the border between my area and Regional Centre 5 and at the time Regional Centre 5 did not have a head of regional centres they only had a deputy. So General DZ tasked me to go in and take command of the operation at the time, bring some of my own verifiers with me and try to bring some order to situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just one other question which you may have answered yesterday but on a matter you've just been dealing with a moment ago. What date was it you actually went on leave so that you weren't there when the mission withdrew on about the 20th of March?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was the 15th of March or something like that. It was a few days before the end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So you were there until the 15th of March or thereabouts --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- and were not aware of any increase in MUP forces, reinforcement from outwith Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And do you know whether, in fact, any of the -- strike that. Are you aware of the fact that Colonel Mijatovic, the MUP liaison to the KVM mission, also personally followed up the local level notifications relating to Racak with a notification to the KVM headquarters the morning of the operation?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, again, not being involved -- first of all, if the notification were sent to the Pristina headquarters of the KVM, that would not normally go to you, in any event.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pristina Regional Centre 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, if I can move on to another locale. I would like to take a few moments to attempt to clear up your testimony about the incident in Rogovo, in Djakovica municipality. First of all, am I correct that you were able to verify beyond any doubt that most of the dead were active KLA fighters in that case?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And isn't it a fact that a fire-fight between the KLA and the Serbian forces occurred around 6.30 in the morning, or in the early morning hours?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the reports -- I think the reports talk about fire-fights that -- the ones that certainly were seen and factual by the verifiers themselves, I think they were closer to about 10.00 in the morning, but there had been some action early as well. So it was an issue of what did we actually witness and hear, and the verifiers on the ground I don't think were there at 6.30 in the morning, but they heard from the villagers and so on that there had been some action early in the morning as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sorry. Again, I'm trying to allow the interpreters and the transcript to catch up with us. In any event, we can be assured that the fighting was protracted in that incident between the two forces.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Protracted meaning short?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Meaning long.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Meaning longer.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think that's the case. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Do you know what time you arrived at the scene?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I arrived somewhere around noon or thereafter, maybe 1300, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And at the time that you arrived and thereafter, a detailed investigation lasting most of the remainder of the day was undertaken by the Serbian authorities. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you know approximately how long that investigation took place?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, certainly that entire day, I believe, and perhaps carried on, you know, later because we were actually looking for the results of that investigation ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And the KVM received a detailed reporting from both the MUP liaison officer and General Loncar regarding the incident and the investigation conducted. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all, I believe General Loncar was on the ground in Rogovo at the time I was there as well. And I believe a report did come through but I don't remember seeing it personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. And, again, the reporting from the Serbian MUP with respect to this incident was in compliance with the various agreements in place?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, with respect to the incident and your personal observations, you did not -- since -- strike that. You could not tell the difference between the various forces, the MUP forces. You couldn't tell what the various units were that were involved, could you?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only way I could tell was the different dress that they were wearing, outfits. Some of them were in the regular dark blue camouflage outfits; some of the personnel on the ground were wearing these one-piece kind of jump-suits that were grey, a greyer colour. And so that's the only thing that I could distinguish certainly in my dealings there on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we could -- I apologise again. I'm not meant to be disrespectful. I'm just trying to catch up with the transcript. With respect to these grey jump-suits, am I correct that in particular the individuals that were moving the bodies and taking photographs were primarily wearing these grey jump-suits and plastic disposable gloves on their hands?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were a number of them walking around the scene. As well, my verifiers saw the body of the dead MUP was wearing one of those grey sweat-suits or grey jump-suits also.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, in your statement, if we could turn to that for that second, at page 3, General, you claim -- you talk about during the time-period of the KVM, that General DZ would meet with General Sreten Lukic on several occasions and that you had replaced General DZ on three such occasions but that General Lukic had been replaced by Colonel Mijatovic. The question I have for you, sir: Are you aware of the fact, as testified to by General DZ, General Loncar and Colonel Ciaglinski here, that in fact the meetings you referenced were with members of the Yugoslav Commission for Cooperation with the KVM and did not involve General Lukic, who was not a member of that commission?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware of the reason why he was not there, but I was quite happy to meet with Colonel Mijatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And in the occasions that you met with Colonel Mijatovic, did you find him to be cooperative with the whole process?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in your statement you refer to General Lukic as a lieutenant-general, and I think he would thank you for the promotion since he was only a major-general or a brigadier-general at the time. But I trust from the limited information and from this misunderstanding we have now cleared up that you, in fact, had a very limited knowledge and were quite unaware of who Mr. Lukic was exactly?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, when dealing with the MUP, if we look at attachment MM/23, specifically annex A. And for purposes of my question, it's general enough that we don't need to go through it with a fine-tooth comb. I'm just trying to place where it's coming from. In the annex A, I note that the information relating to MUP outside of Prizren is rather sketchy. There's very few names of individuals mentioned, et cetera. Do you agree with me that apart from the people that you dealt with in Prizren itself, your knowledge of personnel outside of the area and their role within the MUP was fairly limited?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, that would be a good -- that would be a correct assumption.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, I don't have an MM/23. Am I missing something?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, it might be MM/2B --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: My handwriting is getting the better of me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, if we can return to Sreten Lukic for a moment. Your knowledge of him was limited. Am I correct that you never had a chance to see any official documents setting forth any duties or responsibilities of General Lukic?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And as far as you know, you never met Sreten Lukic?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in -- I apologise. In MM/2 of your statement, specifically paragraph 6 of the same, you describe that you were reporting details to the KVM in Pristina, specifically to the Fusion Centre, which you describe as a black hole. Now, what do you mean when you describe the Fusion Centre as a black hole? Did you -- is it your understanding that information that didn't agree with the -- strike that. Well, did you find that information relating to aggression or violations by the KLA was ignored? Is that what you meant by that term?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not what I meant. I meant that we sometimes found that there was very little feedback on the information that we provided. So it was sort of a one-way flow mostly.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, at page 6 of your statement, the third paragraph from the top, you mention that your MUP counter-part in Prizren, Colonel Vojnovic, was deputy prefect as well as chief of police. What is the basis of your belief that he was deputy prefect and what do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: In fact, I don't exactly recall where I received that information, so -- you know, in fact, this is a piece where I kind of lost the -- you know, where I received from information between now and in 2002 when I first testified, or certainly in 2000 when I gave this statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. Now, when dealing with the MUP, we've got military sounding ranks given to MUP personnel. Am I correct that you, based upon your military experience, would equate that rank structure as being similar to the military but you really don't know whether that's the case?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're right. You're exactly right.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Do you recall who was your police liaison officer in Prizren from the KVM side?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it was a Lieutenant-Colonel Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: On the KVM side?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, my liaison -- on the KVM side? No, I don't recall his name exactly at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: But there was one individual that was tasked --

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was one appointed. I believe it's in my notes and my papers.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I believe it is, too, but the name is escaping me at the moment as well. In any event, with respect to --

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Les House, I believe. Les House.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's the name that's referenced in one of your attachments. With respect to Mr. House, would it be accurate that as your liaison he was in daily contact with the police and daily meetings with the MUP and the police in Prizren?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And the liaison on the SUP side, you mention Mr. Petrovic. I also know of a Mr. Vukobrat. With respect to whomever was the liaison on the SUP side, am I correct that they fully cooperated with the KVM during the time-period they were there?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And you found them to be professional in their interactions with you?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And in addition to the appointed liaison officer, Colonel Vojnovic, also, I guess, informally met with you and assisted you as well. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And did you find him to be professional in his dealings with you?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Again, I'm slowing for the transcript. I apologise. We're getting through this. Now, during your testimony yesterday, you stated that on one occasion you went to a police station - I don't recall if you mentioned where - and that you saw Albanians standing in line looking intimidated. Now, the question I have for you is: Apart from being around the police station, you did not eye-witness the police personnel present at that location being abusive, did you?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And, in fact, you yourself never eye-witnessed a single excess on the part of the police during your stay in Kosovo, did you?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not personally, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Relative to your meetings with Commander Drini of the KLA, in at least two of the notes from these meetings, there's a reference to the missing Serbs that you asked -- or that the KVM asked him about. The notation states that Drini said that if they were missing in his zone, they were probably dead. Did you take this to mean that the KLA was executing Serbian civilians within your zone of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, either executing or that they would have died through action, military action. So, you know, when he would say something like this, that's what I was taking for, you know, granted.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And just a few more points to finish up. Suva Reka was within your zone of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, [Realtime transcript read in error "I didn't"] it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Am I --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think the transcript at page 38, line 15, says the answer is: "I didn't, it was." I believe the general said "Yes, it was."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That one's easy to correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: With respect to the KVM headquarters or centre in Suva Reka, am I correct that it was relocated from the Hotel Boss to a private Albanian residence during the course of the mission?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that is the case, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you, in fact, recall the reason why it was located?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you never visited the MUP staff in Pristina, did you?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Pristina, no, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Yesterday Mr. Marcussen seemed to indicate that your testimony would relate to how the MUP staff in Pristina coordinated activities across the whole of the province of Kosovo-Metohija, but in your statement at the bottom of page 10 you actually state that you have not heard of any such MUP coordination headquarters Pristina. Is that still accurate, though, what you say in your statement at page 10, that you had not heard of any such MUP coordination headquarters in Pristina?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you define a coordination centre as different than just a normal MUP headquarters or -- that's an easy -- if that was what we were trying to do, then I would say that I've not heard of any, you know, like coordination centre outside of the normal headquarters. I certainly would have expected that in Pristina would have been the headquarters of the MUP for the Kosovo region.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: But that's just speculation. You don't know any hard facts?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was never there. I never visited, so I can't confirm one or the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. One final question for you, sir, and this is getting back to the KLA. Did you have any information or knowledge, either directly or through your operatives in the KVM, that the KLA had ordered villagers in Albanian villages, particularly around the border area, to leave those villages in February and March of 1999?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not have any.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General, for your time.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivetic. Any further cross-examination? Mr. Marcussen, re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Just a very limited number of points, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: General, yesterday there was -- and I believe also today, there was some talk about this information that Drini gave you that there was -- at least he said they had a plan to take fighting to towns and things like this. Now, which locations within your regional centre would you define as towns, to start?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you know, it's a bit of a semantic question here. Villages and towns -- I guess if you define a town as slightly bigger than a village, there might have been a few -- for example, the municipalities perhaps would be towns but, you know, I wouldn't go any further than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: But to your knowledge, while you were in Kosovo, was there a KLM -- KLA presence in, for example, Suva Reka, Djakovica, Orahovac, and Prizren?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was a KLA presence -- you know, I can't go city by city and tell you that there was a presence here or a presence there, because sometimes you didn't know who was KLA or where the KLA were or whether they were camouflaged or not. Certainly in the areas where there was a strong Serb authority presence, I would have thought that there would not be a very strong KLA presence. The KLA preferred to be in the outlying kind of -- I think in the regions, you know, the small villages and kind of lost in the woods and that's where they preferred to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: So while you were in Kosovo, the fighting was not taken to the towns. Drini's plan, if there was one, was not implemented?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And I just wanted to clarify your -- the incident with the 35 bodies that you -- that occurred very early after you arrived to maybe even have occurred --

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: -- before you came. So your involvement was in the -- in getting the bodies back to the families?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And you were not offered the location itself where this incident had happened?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Now, we've been talking a bit about the functions and maybe authority of liaison officers and there's just one more point I'd like to try to clarify with you. If a liaison officer enters into an agreement with the person or the body that he's liaising with, would that be a sign that the liaison officer either had the delegated authority that we talked about or that the thing he agreed to had been approved by the chain of command that he was liaising with?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And then about Rogova, when you -- you said you arrived afternoon maybe at 1.00 or something like that. At that point in time when you arrived, had the bodies from the incident been moved?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they had.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Had they been -- where did the bodies you saw --

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they had them lined up, you know -- beside the -- inside the compound in lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And were there any signs that some of them had also been moved on from there to another location?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there had been some that had been moved and left the location already, but I can't exactly recall how many bodies were lined up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Marcussen, which part of the statement is this dealt with?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: It's dealt with in the -- it's dealt with in the Milosevic transcript. I believe it's in parts that were allowed in. Yeah, right now I don't remember whether it's in the -- I don't think it's in the statement, it's only in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: You were also asked whether you yourself had seen excesses by the MUP at police stations and maybe check-points, and you said you did not. Have you any doubts about the correctness of what your verifiers reported to you when they said they had seen this sort of thing?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no doubt.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Excuse me, General. I have a question to ask. This has arisen because of your written statement reflected in paragraph 43 --

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: -- and pertains to the 29th of January, 1999. What are your impressions about this cooperation you had mentioned, both in paragraph 43 and its preceding paragraph, 42, the relationship being cordial with these institutions whose abbreviations are reflected here. And also that -- could you please dilate more on your impressions about what the -- about what you saw and what was the interaction and how these two units, two names, were cooperated with each other. That will be very important for us, coming from a person having high office like yourself and you were also physically there. I'm most grateful.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I guess I would -- I would describe the cooperation as professional, very much required.
