In any -- in any activity, any activity involving the police and the military, there has to be very close cooperation to ensure that each knows what the other is going to do so that there are no friendly engagements from friendly to friendly, if you know what I mean. And all the cases that I saw, I certainly -- my experience was that they -- they cooperated. They seemed to know what each other's plan was. There were clear delineation of responsibilities, but so ensure that there is clear delineation of responsibilities you must do some prior coordination and establish what the delineation will be. So that was my experience certainly in the theatre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Just for further elucidation, now, in paragraph 36, if you -- I would request that you kindly look at paragraph 36 and then see if you could very kindly speak of the relationship.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: My impression -- yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: In terms of paragraph 42 and 43.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: What special things you saw --

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: -- what extraordinary things you saw, what exceptional things you saw, because cooperation generally is one thing and exceptional is the other. What exceptional things you saw?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH OMER MICHEL MAISONNEUVE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would not characterise it as exceptional. What I would tell you is that generally my sense was, my assessment of both those actions was that the VJ would provide perimeter-type support and help while the -- the military forces -- sorry, the police forces would conduct the actual operations in the -- you know, in the close combat, if you wish, or in the tactical piece. So, for example, when it was reported that howitzers were pointed towards Racak, then that would seem to indicate to me as a military officer that the artillery was prepared to support the actual dismounted operation in case there was -- in case there was a -- you know, they ran into trouble, to allow them to eradicate themselves, this type of activity. But I would not call that extraordinary or exceptional. I would call that, you know, understood and agreed to delineation of responsibilities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that completes your evidence, Mr. Maisonneuve. Thank you once again for coming to the Tribunal to give evidence and for your patience while we've dealt with one or two issues that have arisen during the evidence. That completes it, as I say, and you're now free to leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Marcussen, the next witness will be?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: The next witness will be Mr. Kickert, and I believe he would be on his way now, together with Ms. Moeller, who is going to be the counsel taking him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Moeller. Okay. Well, we shall rise now and resume at 11.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Kickert.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration to speak the truth by reading aloud the document which will be placed before you..

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. Ms. Moeller.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Kickert.

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Could you just state your full name for the sake of the transcript, please.

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Jan Kickert.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And what is your nationality?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Austrian.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And what is your occupation?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: I'm a diplomat in the Austrian Foreign Service.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Where are you currently posted?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: In Vienna, in the ministry.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: How long have you been working as a diplomat?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Since 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And during this time, were you ever posted to Serbia and Montenegro?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. I was posted to Belgrade in November 1997.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And how long did you stay in this post?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Until 1999, until the beginning of the NATO bombing.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: I think we have to be careful to pause a little bit between question and answer. That applies for me as well, because we're both speaking in English, so the interpreters can follow us actually.

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: While you were posted to Serbia and Montenegro, which position did you hold in the embassy?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: I was -- I was second secretary in the Austrian Embassy in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And what was your portfolio or what were your specific responsibilities during this time?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: I had a mixed portfolio dealing on the one side with media and cultural issues and on the other hand with political issue of Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And who was the mission chief during this time, Mr. Kickert?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: That was Ambassador Petritsch.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: While posted to Belgrade, did you ever go to Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. I started to go to Kosovo in January 1998 and ever more frequently during 1998 and during the second half of 1998 when Austria hold -- held the rotating EU Presidency I spent almost half of my time in Kosovo and the other half of my time up in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And during your -- during the time you spent in Kosovo, where were you based there?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: In the beginning, the trips were mostly day trips. We would go down from Belgrade, driving to Pristina. My first trips just took me to Pristina and not into the rest of Kosovo, and if I stayed there overnight I would stay in a hotel at the beginning. And from the beginning of July, the Austrian Embassy -- July 1998, the Austrian Embassy had rented a house in Pristina which we used as our base.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And can you tell us a little bit about how the Austrian Embassy came to rent this house.

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: The European Union always wanted to have representation in Pristina, which was not well regarded by the Belgrade authorities. So we then -- as Austria took over the EU Presidency, we just took the initiative to rent a house there on a bilateral level to have a base there, invited the EU organisations who were present which was ECHO, the humanitarian organisation, and the European Commission who dealt with aid projects connected to the education agreement. They were invited to join us in our house to have sort of a EU house, after all.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And you said: "The European Union wanted to have a representation, but this was not well regarded by the Belgrade authorities." Do you know the reason why it wasn't well regarded?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: I mean, my suspicion is that they wanted -- they didn't want to have too much of an international presence in Pristina. The US had an office there. They were -- for historical reasons. I don't know the real background. And we wanted to have -- as EU, a representation there, too. The Belgrade authorities, they the whole time 1998 didn't want to have the Kosovo issue nationalised [Realtime transcript read in error "internationalised"], so maybe that's the background they didn't want us to have a permanent basis in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And what --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Did you -- just one second. You say there that they didn't want the Kosovo issue --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Internationalised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Internationalise, yes. The transcript reflected it wrong. Thank you. Ms. Moeller.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: This residence in Pristina, which flag did you use there?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: That was a bit of an issue. We used to fly one day both the Austrian and the EU flag, and that was the day when the EU troika -- that must have been end of July 1998 -- was visiting Kosovo coming from Belgrade. They had a meeting, the EU troika, led by the Secretary-General of the Austrian foreign ministry Albert Rohan and accompanied by two political directors. That was -- of the UK and of Germany, the outgoing and the incoming EU Presidency. That was Emyr John Perry and Mr. Fischer from Germany. They had a meeting before and I believe it was with foreign minister Jovanovic. And there was quite a debate on this house, and the compromise was then that they would accept it as long as it was on a solely bilateral basis. That's why we took off the EU flag and just had the Austrian flag for the time being.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And while Austria had this residence in Pristina, did the embassy encounter any other problems with this residence in terms of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I wonder, Ms. Moeller, why are we spending so much time on this? What is its relevance to the indictment?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What is the relevance of this --

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: I think it's relevant to show -- it is -- it goes to the interests of Serbia in 1998 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's entirely understandable that Serbia would not want things internationalised in Kosovo. We understand all that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Well, I think the relevance is that when Mr. Petritsch testified there was an issue of efforts made by Serbia to get this situation into grip in 1998, and Mr. Petritsch, I recall, testified that if some more international involvement would have been accepted, it would have been helped to improve the situation and this is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Countries over the world debate the extent to which internationals should be allowed into their affairs. I come from one myself. So it's an issue that we all know is a debatable political issue that we're not here to resolve. Let's get to the issues in the indictment, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: I will, Your Honours. But there is another issue related to this house which goes to -- no, no. It goes to issues that are quite relevant to the case. And if you stay with me for maybe one question, then I'm done with this issue. May I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Mr. Kickert, I asked you whether there were any other problems encountered by the Austrian Embassy with regard to this residence at any time.

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Apart from the flag issue at the beginning, it was only later in the year, end of the year, probably December, that we had a problem with our electricity, when our electricity was turned off because they accused us of tampering the electricity metre and asked from us a back payment and a fine of, I don't know, 10.000, 20.000 Deutschemarks.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And which steps did you - meaning you and the embassy - undertake to resolve this issue, first?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Well, we tried to solve it locally. I personally went to see the head of the ElektroKosovo agency and was not able to resolve it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And were you finally able to resolve it and how?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: That was Ambassador Petritsch bringing this issue up with Mr. Sainovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And what happened then?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Shortly thereafter, the electricity was restored and we didn't have to pay the fine.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you. Moving on now. During your --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I may say, Ms. Moeller, I'm distinctly unimpressed by that being an issue that might be used to indicate the degree of control that Mr. Sainovic had over affairs in Kosovo. But if you think -- I mean, I'm astonished that the Prosecution should think this is relevant to the case.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, it's a mosaic of many pieces that we will attempt to stitch together at the end and it may or may not prove our case. In this regard it's one tiny bit of evidence we think is relevant, but it is of course, up to you to decide that at the end, and I will move on now.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Mr. Petritsch, while you were in Pristina on your -- on your visits there, did you go on any field-trips in the region?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: As I said my first trips were to Pristina alone to meet the political figures which were located in Pristina. It was not until June that I participate -- went to the field participating in an organised field trip organised by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs to western Kosovo. And only thereafter did I start making my own field-trips.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. And in general, which areas did you mainly visit throughout 1998, if you can say?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Would have been central Kosovo, the Drenica area, it would have been western Kosovo, which is called Metohija by the Serbs and Dukagjin by the Albanians.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: I would now like to talk about some field-trips in more detail with you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Your Honours, we have documents we wish to tender in this regard. I have a bundle here which I would like to give to the witness. It contains both the English and the German original. He asked in the proofing that he would have a chance to refer to the German original in court. May I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Okay, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: -- hand this to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: It is in the order, Mr. Kickert, in which we will go through the documents, which is in a chronological order. You already mentioned that your first field-trip took place in June, I think. Before that, was there any field-trip organised, to your knowledge, already in which you did not participate - you meaning again you and the Austrian Embassy?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Yes, there was after the incident in Prekaz beginning of March 1998 that a trip was organised by the foreign ministry to visit the site of Prekaz. That must have been just a few days later, early March 1998.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And did anyone from the Austrian Embassy take part in this trip?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And why was that?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: We were afraid, and most of the EU countries also follow that line, is that we were afraid that that would be misused as a -- for propaganda purposes. So we didn't want to get involved in that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Could you explain that what you mean by misused for propaganda purposes.

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Well, that -- that they would show us the locality and say, Well, this is -- this is a legitimate fight against terrorists, as they were calling them, and that by showing on TV us, Western diplomats there, they were portrayed in a way that we would approve of their action.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Now can we call up exhibit P2666, please. And English version, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: This exhibit should be the first document in the bundle that you have, Mr. Kickert. And it is dated 8 June 1998. If you could look at that. Is that one of the reports you drafted?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, because in the right top corner it says: "SB," which is [German spoken]. That means not literally, but it means author, that was myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And this report refers to a trip for diplomats and military attaches in the first paragraph under the bullet point on 7 June to the battle zones around Decani and western Kosovo and it says that you represented the embassy. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: It also says the participants were mainly junior diplomats?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: On behalf of the EU states yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And then the route travelled is explained in the third paragraph. Can you comment on the fact that the route taken was not the most direct route actually to go through these locations?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Yeah, the most direct route would have been on the route which goes from Pristina to Pec, and we took a big detour to the north to -- even into Rozaje, which is Montenegro, to get to Pec.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And why was this detour taken at the time?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: This question was also posed I believe by the Japanese ambassador who participated, and the reason was for security. Our assessment was that the Belgrade authorities didn't have full control of the direct road between Pristina and Pec at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Now I would like to turn to page 2 of this report --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The report actually says that the Serb authorities have no control over the road between Pristina and Pec. Is that different from your impression?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, what I've written is that apparently without control. That's in the first bullet of the -- of the -- at the very first bullet on top of the report --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can we go back to the previous page, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, at the summary. I say [German spoken] apparently without control. So I had no direct information, but the fact that we took this large detour and not the direct road was for us an indication that they felt not secure enough to take us on this direct road.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Now, since we're back to the first page I may as well address one of the bullet points. It's the third from the bottom, the third-last one, saying: "Situation in Decani tense, majority of inhabitants appear to have left." How did you make this conclusion or finding?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think we need to go back to page 2 of the document now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We drove there with our convoy, I think it was two buses, and we got off in Decani. And the only people we met were in a cafe sitting outside drinking coffee, and we chatted with them. Some were from a village more in the south called Baboloc, which were refugees from elsewhere outside Kosovo. And the houses -- and you didn't see any people either on the street nor in the windows of houses. So the appearance was that this town, Decani, was pretty empty.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And you describe that on page 2 of your report under the name Decani. And then under that you say: "Next village Prilep." How about inhabitants in Prilep, how was the situation in this village?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: We got off there too, as far as I recall, and wandered around. And I can't recall any inhabitants there either, or if so, just a few.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And you also refer in your report to considerable devastation, and in the paragraph dealing with Decani, the third on the second page, you say: "Considerable devastation but by no means as drastic as described by LDK." Can you comment on that and explain it further.

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Yeah, one of the problems we had all along was a question of getting accurate information. So we got information either from the Belgrade authorities or from Kosovo, from the LDK, who had their daily bulletin and so on. And one of the reasons we decided to participate in that field-trip is to see for ourselves the effects of the military actions in the Decani area. And what I've described here is that the LDK said as a -- in Vukovar, and I've been to Vukovar and seen the destruction there, and it was not comparable to the destruction I've seen in Decani.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And What kind of destruction that you called considerable devastation did you see yourself, if you could describe it, how the cities looked.

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: As I also write in the report there was some direct impact you could see, and I'm not a military expert whatsoever, but I had military attaches who I could ask. And there were some rounds of heavy ammunition but mostly it was machine-gun fire. And what was -- what was interesting, remarkable, is that a lot was destroyed by fire.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. You also in the last sentence of the paragraph dealing with Decani, you refer to: "Colleagues who visited the Drenica region in March reported comparitively little destruction, no shelling with heavy weaponry." Who were these colleagues who had been to Drenica in March?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: That must have been military attache colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And how did they describe the destruction in Drenica in March?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: They probably talk about Prekaz where they had heavier weaponry used than apparently in the Decani region.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Now, at the bottom of page 2 there is a title saying: "Briefing by Yugoslav Foreign Ministry and the Ministry of the Interior." Do you recall who briefed the group of diplomats on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: No, I don't have a clear recollection of who exactly the people were. I remember that we were accompanied by people from the foreign ministry and the Ministry of the Interior, but I cannot state with any certainty who these people were any more.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And the second bullet point is an entry that I would also ask you to comment on. "The visit should rectify erroneous information of the international community figures for refugees fleeing to Albania 'totally false.'" Can you explain that bullet point a little bit?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Yeah, throughout 1998 and really first half of 1998, because of the security incidents and the response, we had a number of IDPs throughout Kosovo and apparently there was a claim that many fled to Albania, which at this briefing the Belgrade authorities refuted.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: I now would like to move on --

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Unless Your Honours have any questions about this particular exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: -- to the next one, Exhibit P2665. This is a report of the 1st of July, 1998, and is it correct, Mr. Kickert, you are the author again, as it shows: "SB: Kickert" on the top again?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: In the summary it says: "Official confirmation for the first time of participation of army units in inland operations." Let me ask you first, before the 1st of July did you have any information on whether and to which extent, if so, the VJ was participating in any anti-terrorist operations in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: No, we didn't have any information. It was an issue we brought up with our Austrian military attache time and again in the first half of 1998, and his assessment was that the VJ was not involved in these actions. They may have provided some logistics, trucks, whatever, but they were not directly involved in the fighting.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Now, this report in the second paragraph under the summary refers to: "HO press reports." Can you explain what the HO means?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: HO is a bureaucratic abbreviation. [German spoken], that means local in this respect, so local press information.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: So this was based on local press releases only or did you have any other information about that facts stated in this document at the time?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Only -- I do cite Reuters here, so that's the only source of information I had writing this paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Did you later gain any more information about the degree of participation of the VJ in operations in Kosovo after the 1st of July?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Not that I can recall now.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Okay. The next exhibit would be P2664.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Now, Your Honour, I have an objection to P2665 and its use in this trial. It's based on press reports. It's not anything based on first-hand knowledge. I know your ruling is to say to the extent that it's used with the witness, but clearly, it's based on local press, some of which is reported in Reuters. So the observation I wish to make is that P2665 is nothing more than a summary of what Mr. Kickert found in the local press.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Which exhibit is on the screen at the moment? Can we go back to 2665, please. Do we have a problem?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You may have used this exhibit already, Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honours. That's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I have a marvelous memory, you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I asked if some of the information in it was correct. I didn't rely on the exhibit, Your Honour. I put it to the previous witness, asking about information at the conclusion of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You can take it that evidence confined to a press report of the involvement of the VJ in operations anywhere will carry no weight with us. You can move now to 2664.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Mr. Kickert, 2664 is a report dated 6 July 1998 and the subject is "Kosovo Observer Mission Inaugural Trip." Can you explain the background to that document a little bit.

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Well, first, I've written it in English because as we took over -- Austria took over the EU Presidency on the 1st of July, it was also our obligation to inform other EU member states about what was going on. So I drafted it in English, in the form of a CorEu, which is a form of communication between EU member states. And the whole event was inauguration of the Kosovo Diplomatic Observer Mission. This was an agreement with the Belgrade authorities that we would put observers into the field to get first-hand information of what was going on in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And did you participate in this field-trip?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And Mr. Petritsch, was he also there?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Yes, he was also there. We drove down from Belgrade, made this field excursion, if you like, and then drove to Belgrade the very same day.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Now, on page 2 of this exhibit, the route that was taken is described: From Pristina north to Kosovska Mitrovica, Gornja Klina, Srbica up to Donji Prekaz and the Jashari family compound. What observations, if any, did you make on this field-trip?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Well, as I describe just a sentence later on, we did not enter any UCK-controlled areas at the time. And I remember that we stopped in Srbica and there was a police -- not a check-point, but where they protected themselves against possible attacks. We chatted with the policemen and they told us about sporadic fire, but they didn't seem too much concerned about attacks after all.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And do you know why the convoy did circumvent all UCK-controlled areas?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: This is what I write at the end in German, is that it was the insistence or the wish of the Russian ambassador not to enter any territory which was UCK controlled, or he didn't want to have an encounter with the UCK.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, in this very month, in July 1998, did you participate in any other field-trips?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Yeah, this is -- in July, this is when I started to travel more, and July was also the month where we went with political directors of EU troika. This was the month where Mr. Rohan was visiting on his own. This is also the month where I went to Malisevo and met for the very first time Mr. Thaqi.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Maybe we can take this one after one because we don't have the documents here on these trips. The field-trip with the political directors of the EU troika, who was participating in this mission?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Chronologically, that was the last of the three trips, but participating was, as I said before, the political director of the United Kingdom, Emyr John Perry, and the political director of the German foreign ministry, Wolfgang Ischinger. And from Austria, the Presidency was the Secretary-General Albert Rohan and -- yeah. So these are the top people who participated.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And where did you travel on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: We travelled on the normal western road to Pec.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And any specific observations you made during this field-trip?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: We were stopped at a police check-point and were not let through. And I remember that we tried to talk the policeman, saying, "Well, this is an important delegation and they're going to see Mr. Milosevic the very next day." That did not impress the policemen there. They just started to radio back to headquarters when Mr. Rohan said that we just had met Mr. Odalovic, Veljko Odalovic, and he had guaranteed us freedom of movement throughout Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Who was Mr. Veljko Odalovic?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: He was the prefect of Pristina, but for us he was -- we treated him as the prefect for the whole of Kosovo. So any diplomat who would go down to Pristina to meet Kosovo Albanians would also normally meet Veljko Odalovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And in terms of the areas you passed through on this trip, did you observe anything in particular?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: This was a time when you would see, time and again, houses burning, unharvested fields burning. And with this impression also the political directors went back to Belgrade and confronted Mr. Milosevic with what they had seen.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: So did you see that yourself?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: You also mentioned a field-trip to Malisevo.

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Can you elaborate on that a little bit.

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: There were two trips. One was with Mr. Rohan, who came by himself. That was before the EU troika. And through ECMM, that's the European Community Monitoring Mission, I just want to explain that we had this monitoring mission in ex-Yugoslavia for quite a while and also in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. And from May on, we had one team located in Kosovo reporting to us. So they were already quite acquainted with the area, and through them we had organised a trip to Malisevo to meet for the first time UCK officials.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And what was the reason for this meeting with UCK officials?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: The reason was to convince them to be included in the political process. We feared that the violent clashes would grow, that violence would prevail, and so the initiative was taken by Secretary-General Rohan to make an effort by seeing somebody in the leadership of the UCK to involve them in the political process. It was not easy because we didn't know the structure of the UCK whatsoever, but we made an effort.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And you said that was the first time that such meeting was arranged for. Were there other meetings in 1998 that you attended with the UCK, the KLA?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Just to be precise, it was the first meeting we had with the KLA. The Americans did have meetings, even if they were said to be incidental, with the KLA. I remember a meeting of Mr. Holbrooke in Junik where he was even in pictures with armed KLA people. But to our knowledge, afterwards this person he met there was not of importance, not in the leadership of the KLA. But there were contacts also on other levels by the US.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for this clarification. Now, from your side, from the side of the Austrian government, were there any follow-up meetings after this one in July 1998 with KLA representatives?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Yeah. Later in July, it must have been end of July, I did also go with my British colleague David Slinn to Klecka, to meet in Klecka with the spokesperson, as he was labelled, of the KLA, Jakup Krasniqi. Also at that meeting were Ram Buja and also Fatmir Limaj.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Okay. And any other meetings you would have attended with KLA representatives?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: That was the last meeting for quite some time, because this is the period where the summer offensive of the Serb security forces had started. The KLA, that was -- from their attempt to take Orahovac; then the KLA abandoned Malisevo and went to the hills. So it was, for us, not possible to arrange any meetings with them any more for quite some time.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Now, going back to Malisevo, you say the KLA abandoned Malisevo. What was the -- did Malisevo have any particular significance for the KLA?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Well, the time when I was there in July, they portrayed it as the capital of the "free territories," as they called it, under quotation marks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You said something about Orahovac there which has not been very well transcribed. Could you say again what you told us about Orahovac.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My take of Orahovac is that the KLA not -- being a little bit -- misjudging their strength, tried to take Orahovac and were repelled by the Serb security forces. The way the KLA presented it is that they were provoked to go into there, but my take is that they just overestimated their strength at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Moeller.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Did you visit Orahovac during 1998?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Very often.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And for which purpose, if any specific?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: The purpose was -- so after this counter-offensive, our main aim was on the return of IDPs, and Orahovac was one of the areas where we wanted people to return. The tensions were very high. This is a mixed -- this is an ethnically mixed city, Serbs and Albanians and -- so we wanted to facilitate the return of people to Orahovac and the surrounding, not only the city itself. So what we were doing is then what was called then, because they officially launched it, the foreign minister of Germany and the foreign minister of France, the Kinkel-Vedrine initiative, is to, through the presence of our European Union monitoring mission in Orahovac, give some confidence that the situation has calmed down. We had to be careful not to give them the feeling that we were responsible for security but to give them confidence through the presence of internationals that there would be some observation of what was going on. And it did have some effect; the people had returned to Orahovac. We tried then later to copy this model to other areas, which is much more difficult if it's not a city. So we had this project later on in Kishna Reka --

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes. We'll get to that later. Thank you. How was the -- about what time would these initiatives have been taken in 1998, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: That must have been August 1998, starting August 1998.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And did you - meaning, again, the Austrian Embassy representatives and the ECMM teams - have free access to the area in Orahovac?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: That varied. Time and again we would be -- we would be turned back at check-points, Serb check-points, and other times we had no problem whatsoever to go wherever we wanted. This varied and it was sometimes pure luck. Sometimes there was an operation going on and they didn't want us to get in there, also for security reasons. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And you mentioned a little bit earlier that you went to Malisevo twice and we talked about the field-trip with the EU troika representatives. Which was the other trip you made?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Malisevo is a little town which -- a town which is at a crossroads, so you would -- it's easy to go through Malisevo in whichever direction you come from, the north or the east or the west or the south. So you would pass through Malisevo very frequently if you travelled through Kosovo. So during the summer, many, many times we went through to Malisevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And what, if anything, did you recognise in regard to Malisevo over this summer period?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: What was striking was that immediately after the abandonment of Malisevo by the KLA and of the local population, it was an empty city with just Serb police stationed there and a few elderly people maybe having remained. And you could witness, every time you would go through, that there was more destruction in the city, until this town was even partly leveled.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if you were to -- if you were asked to summarise your observations in regard to the villages and cities you passed by during your field-trips in July and early August 1998, how would you summarise that?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: My own observations, and especially the observations of our monitors on the ground, is that the houses along the roads and in towns were burnt down rather systematically.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And did you have any information on who was responsible for this destruction and burning of --

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Well, if you would go through a village and there were no inhabits and just Serb security forces, you ask yourself, Who is responsible for that? Our observers, ECMM observers, also witnessed a policeman setting fire to a house, a policeman in uniform. They wrote it in one of their reports.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Okay. I would now like to move on to Exhibit P2655 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before you do that, have I wrongly understood that your last visit around that time was in July?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My last visit where I met KLA people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ah. So in August you still were visiting the locality.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Exhibit P2655.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Mr. Kickert, if you could have a look at that. The first paragraph -- we already looked at that document with Ambassador Petritsch, so it's already been seen by the Judges. But I would like to ask you to give some background about the first paragraph which refers to the freedom of access for humanitarian NGOs. Was there a problem with this freedom of access at that time? And the date is early August, 4 August 1998 here.

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Yes. As I said before, we had problems of access at times, and we didn't go every day to the field. The humanitarian NGOs, they did, and they were turning to us to ask for political support. And as I see there, the bullet points for the demarche, they also complain about radio equipment being confiscated and issues like that. So this is based on the humanitarian organisations turning to us to support them politically so that they could do their job on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Can you name some of these humanitarian organisations who reported these kinds of problems?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Our main interlocutors on the ground were ICRC and UNHCR, but there were also some Western NGOs active on the ground. Medecins Sans Frontieres, Oxfam, these are the ones who were also present in Kosovo also -- before and also during this time.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Now, moving on to page 2 of this exhibit, the speaking points start with a list of major concerns. What was the basis you - meaning, again, you, the embassy, and the colleagues you address in this telefax - heard about these allegations? What was the information underlying these allegations set out under major concerns?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: These were our observers or monitors on the ground. And we got -- from ECMM we got daily reports, weekly reports. This Kosovo Diplomatic Observer Mission, they had joint trips into the field. So there was a US component, there was a Russian component, and there was some joint reports, but I relied, or we relied, mainly on our own European Union monitors.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And which of these points listed could you also know from your own observations during your field-trips?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: As I said before, unharvested fields burning, houses burning. I don't know whether I'd seen IDPs at that time already, but there we relied on the international organisations, mainly UNHCR. We didn't rely on local sources on that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And why didn't you rely on local sources in regards to numbers of refugees?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Because we had the experience also, but we were fearing that they were inflated, the numbers.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And local organisations who would also provide numbers, would you be able to name any?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Well, there was the Mother Teresa Society and there was this Council for Defence of Human Rights and Freedoms. But, as I said, we rather relied on information we got from international NGOs and international organisations.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in August 1998, was there any other field-trip you participated in?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Yeah, time and again. I don't -- yeah, there were several field-trips in August, also in September.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Did you ever meet Emma Bonino in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Yes, she was coming in the second half of August. She was from the European Commission, the commissioner for humanitarian aid. She was visiting and I was co-organising that visit, because we also had the infrastructure, the house, there, where she gave also her press conference. And we were touring Kosovo also with her. Ambassador Petritsch was also present. He was present with her in Belgrade when I was already down in Pristina, and then they flew down and we made this field-trip which was mainly organised by ECHO in conjunction -- ECHO, the European Community Humanitarian Office, in conjunction with UNHCR.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And where did you go on this trip with Ms. Bonino?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: We also went to Malisevo and then we wanted to go to an IDP camp which was east of Malisevo. So if you take the road, the eastern road from Malisevo, you would turn up to the left, meaning to the north, and there our convoy, which was also full of media people, was not let through by -- at a KLA check-point. So we returned and went instead to the northern, Drenica, region to Cirez.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And what, if anything, did you see in Cirez?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: To be honest, I can't recall. There must have been some IDPs for the simple reason that the commissioner was taken there, but that -- no recollection.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: The next exhibit is Exhibit P564, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: I understand, Mr. Kickert, that this is also authored by you, this report?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And it now takes us to September 1998. That was a field-trip in which you participated?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Yes. It was a visit of Ambassador Parak, who was the head of the ECMM. At that time each Presidency had -- was heading the ECMM which had its headquarters for the whole region of ex-Yugoslavia in Sarajevo, so it was based in Sarajevo. And he came down to look at the situation himself. With the logistical assistance of ECMM, we went into the field, if you so like.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And the route you took, as described in the first paragraph, was Pristina-Pec-Decani-Junik-Pec-Pristina. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Now, this document contains some observations, and the first bullet point reads: "Villages along the main Pristina-Pec road are, with the exception of Serbian villages, no longer inhabited." How did you know Albanian villages from Serb villages?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Well, first you can tell quite often by the way the houses are built, the compounds are built. Then you can guess if there's a mosque there that it's -- it will not be a Serbian village. In a Serbian village you would find an Orthodox church. And in this case, by then you could judge, by the degree of destruction and by the number of people being there, whether it was an Albanian or not. So if the village was destroyed and no villagers seen, then you could guess with quite a certainty that it was an Albanian village. And in others you would find -- in Serbian villages you would find people. And I remember one of these crossings from Pristina to Pec. I even saw villagers in civilian clothes with Kalashnikovs for their -- I assume, their own protection. And this would also give you a clue that it was a Serbian village, if they can run around with a Kalashnikov openly.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: You say "... run around with a Kalashnikov openly." Were there any Serb security forces in the area where you saw that, or, I mean --

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: At that particular time when I saw this villager, no. But as I write in this report, there we saw a convoy of milicija.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And that's actually the next bullet point. On 10th September you saw a convoy of military vehicles carrying special army units southwards from Pec. Now, you already mentioned that you are not a military expert. How were you able to conclude that these were special army units that you saw?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: That was certainly based on the assessment of the ECMM observers. Many of the ECMM observers were military. So I would rely on what they told me because I have no idea to see on -- whatever they have on their -- marks on their uniforms, I had no clue whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Were some of these observers also on this field-trip with you and Ambassador Parak?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Absolutely. There must have been at least two cars. The driver most probably was Austrian military and they would always go with military people.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And just to go back for one question, to the first bullet point. The villages along the main Pristina-Pec road, how many villages are we talking about, if you can recall, where you made this observation?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: I don't know how many villages are on the way. I don't know. A dozen? I wouldn't -- I wouldn't be able to make a guess which would hold.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This document is reflecting your own personal observations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But if I may add, a lot comes also from my talk with people who have been in the area. Like, I cite the Dutch military attache --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. You indicate, though, when that is the case, don't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Now moving on to the third bullet point, Junik. You say: "There is nothing to be seen of the 1.000 people who have returned home from the Serbian side." Can you comment on that. Which 1.000 people were those?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: I suppose that that was sort of the claim, that a thousand people had returned to the area. I don't think that Junik had any Serbian -- major Serbian population, so it must have been Albanian. So my interpretation now is that they claim that a thousand people had returned, and I state there that I haven't seen many people, certainly not a thousand people. But then I continue, saying that US KDOM had reported about 2.000 returnees and so we had tasked the ECMM team, which was based in Pec, to verify these reports.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And the next paragraph deals with the Serbian humanitarian centre in Decani. You say: "It was set up, equipped, opened, but nobody went there. The Albanian population did not return." What is your explanation for that fact?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Well, lack of confidence of being able to return, lack of confidence to use the Serbian humanitarian centres, which was not only in Decani but, as I told you about, the return project to Orahovac, they had one there, too. And if they would not go there, the Albanian population, it didn't make much sense to have them the way they were set up.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Were there any ECMM monitors also placed at this or close to this humanitarian centre in Decani?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Yeah, we had -- the ECMM had a different concept. We didn't have the security issues as the Americans had it. The Americans always do this in compounds for security reason. We were regionally dispersed, so the nearest ECMM office was in Pec. And we had one in Prizren, we had one in Kosovska Mitrovica, we had one in Pristina, and I believe so -- later on in Orahovac and later on also in Urosevac/Ferizaj.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: But not in Decani, I conclude from that?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Not to my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: It was near to Pec anyways. You could drive down there easily and they were patrolling the area. So they would go there, I suppose -- every one of these ECMM posts had two teams, so I suppose that they went daily through Decani.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Now, moving on to page 2 of this exhibit. The first bullet point on this side, you refer to an ICRC aid convoy not being allowed entry on the 10th of September nearby Krusevac, that is, I think. Can you comment on that further?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Well, the issue here was always to reach the IDPs, and since there were operations - I called them clean-up operations or mop-up operations - that were going on, the issue was having access to them to give them humanitarian goods, and to find them because they would also move. And I refer to that the ECMM went to Krusevac and didn't see any persons any more there. And the assumption was maybe they moved further south.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Now, the summary of this document states that the number of internally displaced persons has not yet dropped, that they are only being shifted locally by the action of the security forces. What was the underlying information of this conclusion?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Well, the information we got from ECMM and from humanitarian organisations in the field.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And around that time, in early September, did you talk about this problem with Serbian authorities, you meaning again the Austrian Embassy side?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: That was a regular issue with the Belgrade authorities. As you have picked out, this demarche in early August, that continued the discussion with the Belgrade authorities all along because we had this big fear that this will drag on into winter and we would have then pictures around the world of IDPs in the open and freezing in the snow and we just wanted to avoid that. And I think also Belgrade understood that and was receptive to our efforts like the one in Orahovac for people to return and have access to humanitarian organisations.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And in return -- in regard of numbers that you gave to Serbian authorities, how would they respond to that?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: I -- the general was that they were playing down the numbers, and just to not portray it as drastic as it was; on the other hand, you had the Albanian -- Kosovo Albanian side trying to inflate the numbers. So we had the find the middle ground, and this is where we relied very much on UNHCR.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Now, the last bullet point states that entry for humanitarian organisations will be more difficult from now on."

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: No. In German it says: "Continues to be hindered -- the access for humanitarian organisations -- [German spoken] is continuously hindered. That's a wrong translation, then.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours, so I can -- being a German native speaker, I can confirm that the correct translation would be what Mr. Kickert just said is "continuing to be hindered" instead of "will be more difficult from now on." And that would actually resolve my question because then it's not getting more difficult, which I wanted to ask why.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Okay. Then we can move on to the next exhibit which is P558. And this is a document from the end of September, and again, Mr. Kickert, I think you were the author of this document?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And what is this report based on? Is it your own experience or is it reflecting something else?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: No. This is a report based on what my British colleague with whom I shared a lot of work down in Kosovo told me. I couldn't participate in that trip, but I did visit the area earlier in September with him. This is what I'm referring to, to the earlier report of the 7th of September.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And just to give some background, what was this topic of a local police force that is being dealt with in this document? What was it about?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: It was one of the issues to, A, give security -- a sense of security to the people; and B, have it sort of locally owned, meaning that in Kosovo Albanian villages there would be Kosovo Albanian security instead of Serbian police, which should then also facilitate the confidence and the wish to return or stay there.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And where did this initiative come from?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: That originated in Belgrade, but I -- it could be well based on discussions the Americans had with -- in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And before we go back to this document, you mentioned that you went to the place mentioned in the document, Djakovica, on an earlier occasion.

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And was this in relation to this issue of a local police?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. We wanted to see it for ourselves. And I think after we picked up news that this was being -- being done in the area of Djakovica, my British colleague, David Slinn, and I, we went there and we talked to a deputy and not the prefect of Djakovica at the time. And he confirmed it. There was a little bit of uncertainty whether they would be uniformed or armed, and so this is the follow-up report based on what my British colleague told me when he was in the area.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: So what did the deputy of the Prefect of Djakovica tell you at that earlier meeting that they were planning to do?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: That it would set up security, coordinators, or local police in a number of villages of the Djakovica area. At that time, he -- as I said, he was not certain whether they would have uniforms or get side-arms, but in this report I think it -- it says already -- that was then the Prefect of Djakovica -- told my British colleague that they would get uniforms, they would get side-arms and ammunition the very next day, so the 25th of September.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And then your report states in the paragraph before the paragraph titled [German spoken] in German and "verdict" in English?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: "Verdict" is wrong.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Which is also a wrong translation, right?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: It would be assessment.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Exactly. But the paragraph above the "assessment" paragraph refers to a tour of Djakovica via Ponosevac and Junik, that none of the people listed was to be found in any of the villages, despite inquiries being made?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Yes, this was a trip of the British colleague and he was given a list of these security coordinators. So he just hit the road and went to these villages where the people were listed and he didn't find them.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Just to clarify, on this particular tour where none were found, that was only your British colleague or were you with him?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: No, I was not with him. I stayed up there. I had to write a report of the heads of mission on the implementation of the education agreement.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And the observation that most villages were empty of inhabitants, only a very small number of people had returned even to Junik is then also the observation of your British colleague?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Now, turning to the part which should be under the title "assessment." The assessment is -- I think let's first go to the last sentence, because there's also a translation mistake in there that you pointed out when we looked at the document in the proofing. The last sentence says: "For the time being it can only be viewed as a cover-up operation."

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Alibi action, I said. It's sort of -- our assessment was it's nothing -- this action is nothing serious. It was just announced and they did a little bit but it had no real effect on the ground, because I write earlier that the local LDK representatives were saying these locally hired people were police informants, so it would not be giving what -- what the expectation was, meaning confidence, to the local population. Quite the contrary.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And the assessment that it was more or less an alibi operation, was that -- is that now your assessment in this report or is it the assessment that your British colleague gave to you?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: It's a shared assessment.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And as far as you shared this assessment, was it based only on the report of your British colleague or on other information as well?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: And my previous trip when I was, earlier in September, with him there, on the 6th or 7th of September.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Did anything make you reconsider this assessment at a later point? Did you learn anything different in regards to local police?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Well, at end of September things have just -- were taken over by events. This was -- September 1998 was the time of the Secretary-General's report on the implementation of Security Council Resolution - what was that? - 1199, and so there was a lot of activities going on at the end of September/early October, where the discussions were -- Richard Holbrooke was in Belgrade and which resulted in the Kosovo Verification Mission. So we didn't follow this up, to my knowledge, because it was overtaken by events with the KVM and -- or before the KVM was operational, the expanded KDOM.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Now I would like to move on to Exhibit P557.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: This is a document from the 30th of September, 1998. And on the right-hand corner you see under "SB," which means -- as you said in English, would read "author." "MC Kickert Senfter." What would MC be?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Mission chief.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: So it was a common report.

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: It was a joint report. I mean, if I'm the author, he still signs it off and would make changes or additions. But in this report it is a compilation of three authors for the simple reason that I was not present at this talk Ambassador Petritsch had with the Contact Group ambassadors, with President Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Okay. So you already answered my next question. You were not present in the meeting with Milosevic, but I would still like you to look at the last bullet point under the category "Talks with President Milosevic," which took place according to this report on 28 September. And the last bullet point says: "There are perhaps a maximum of 700 IDPs in the open air." Do I understand correctly that this is information that was given by President Milosevic at the time?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Yes, that's how I understand it, that President Milosevic said, "700 IDPs under open air."

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to object to this line of questioning. The witness has said he wasn't present at the meeting. The person who was present at this meeting testified a couple of days ago. That's when the question should have been put, not to this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think it was put, Mr. O'Sullivan, or do you remember it not having been put?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: This witness can't speak to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand the point you're making. But was Petritsch not actually asked?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Your Honours, the document was tendered through Mr. Petritsch.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah. So what's the point in asking this witness about it?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: I just would like him to comment on the number of 700 IDPs in relation to the knowledge he had.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, do that, but don't ask him whether the source is Mr. Milosevic because we've already had the witness that could deal with that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: That was just to clarify where it came from.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Mr. Kickert, this number of 700 IDPs that was stated on this occasion, what do you say about that?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Well, in the report, it continues that the very next day we had been together with the Contact Group ambassadors to an IDP camp in Kisna Reka, which I was referring to before, and on my own account I was there. I would have guessed that in this particular main camp we had been at there were a thousand IDPs alone in this particular camp, and this was a camp in the open.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And this would be referred to in your report under number 2, the second paragraph. Is that the camp you refer to now?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Okay. Do you know how long this camp was there at Kishna Reka?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: All through summer. Most probably at the moment that the KLA had to leave the area, the people would have been withdrawn up. So I guess end of July/early August.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: We can move on to the next exhibit, which is P561.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: I'm just going back a little bit in time, 8 September, and you are the author of this document, Mr. Kickert, are you?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: It refers to a briefing, personal briefing, given to Ambassador Petritsch by the US Assistant Secretary for Democracy, Human Rights, and Labour, Mr. Shattuck. Were you present in this briefing?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: I must have been since I wrote it, but it didn't make much impression on me so I ...

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: I would like to look at the paragraph at the bottom of this document under "Forensic Experts."

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And if you could explain to us what is stated in there, that "Shattuck demonstrated guarded optimism; Milosevic had given him to understand that individual international experts may be considered; he ... ruled out sending in organisations." And then it says: "Shattuck showed interest in either the Finnish team or the Dutch experts." What is that all about, please?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: To get credible information about incidents, claims of massacres, we wanted to have international experts look at certain incidents and so we had the idea of early on to ask -- early on meaning that -- I know that it was already a claim of my foreign minister Wolfgang Schuessel when he in Belgrade visited on the 5th of June, 1998, to ask for international forensic experts to investigate and look at these incidents to get an objective information because you had claims and counter-claims on all these incidents. And we just wanted to get a clear picture about it. So we had proposed this Finnish forensic team which we - meaning Austria - were well-acquainted with through cooperation in Bosnia. And we understood the reluctance of Belgrade not to have the ICTY investigating. So we thought that maybe a way out would be international experts from a neutral country which had no interests and stakes in Kosovo or the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And how was the reaction of Belgrade, as you said, to that -- or the Yugoslav officials to that proposal in June 1998?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Ignorance. I mean, there was no follow-up to that. They said that, Well, we have our own investigations into these. We are a sovereign state. We will have our investigating judges. We have our own pathologists, our own experts look at the issues.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I see the time. Would you like to break at this point?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Kickert, we have to break at this stage for an hour. The usher will show you where you should go to wait for that hour and then you should return. But meanwhile would you leave the courtroom with the usher. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And we shall resume at quarter to 2.00. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.45 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Moeller.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Mr. Kickert, before the break we left off talking about the forensic expert team. Did this forensic team or any forensic team eventually arrive in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And what team was it?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: It was the Finnish team.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And when did it arrive?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: We got the go-ahead by Belgrade at the beginning of October, and they came for their first fact-finding mission in the second half of October, 20th-25th, around that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And how did it come about that they were -- that they were called to come into Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: I think that it was part of the - as I may call it - Holbrooke package. It was for Belgrade certainly the lesser evil than having the ICTY there. It was better to have the forensic -- Finnish forensic experts on what was then a rather bilateral level. We dealt a lot with the circumstances how they were invited. First Belgrade wanted to have them invited by an institution like the Forensic Institute, but we then convinced Belgrade that it would be a formal invitation by a foreign minister -- a letter to the Finnish foreign minister asking to send this team to the FRY.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And what was the mandate of this forensic team? What were they supposed to do once in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: They -- the idea was - and there was a little bit of a haggling about the mandate. We insisted that they should have totally free hand, free movement, and doing investigations as they saw fit. They did arrive. They started their work. We had agreed then on a number of sites and incidents they would look at. We shared them equally, meaning equally in the sense of having some -- some cases where Belgrade alleged an atrocity had happened like Klecka, like Glodjane. And on the other hand we had incidents, same number, where the Kosovo Albanian side alleged to have that -- alleged that the atrocities had happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And which role, if any, did you play in regard to the work of the Finnish expert team?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Well, I was sort of an intermediary. I was the representative of the EU Presidency. They had started off on a bilateral level, the first visit paid by the Finnish government, but then we had a joint action of the European Union, community at the time, where it was commonly paid by the EU.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And after they arrived in Kosovo, what did this team do?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: They set up a headquarters there. They had contacts, both in Belgrade with the authorities and then in Kosovo with the authorities. They had made contact with the Serbian forensic experts, sort of -- then making decisions which sites they would be looking into, issues like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And you said there was a little bit of haggling about the incidents which they would look at. Did they eventually start investigations on certain incidents?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Yes, they did, but they were not able to do their work in the way it was intended to. We had problems -- and that was already back in December then, had problems of doing the exhumations as foreseen at -- of those victims of the alleged incident in Gornje Obrinje.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And what problems were these?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: This was a question of access combined with -- with security. It was no problem whatsoever to go there by themselves, the Finns by themselves, in the company of the ECMM. But when the exhumations should have started, I don't know, around 10th of December or whatever, there was not only the Serbian investigating judge part of the convoy but a long tail of MUP police cars and unit including APCs. And Gornje Obrinje was in the Drenica region in the UCK-held area at that time, so had we continued, it would have meant a conflict, meaning it would have been shooting, for sure, and we, the Finns and I, would have been in the middle of it. So we -- or it was actually myself who then decided we cannot continue and cannot move into this area.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: So you were present when the Finnish forensic team went to Gornje Obrinje, I understand from what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Yes. They had the most logistical support by ECMM. We even had the big trucks. Everything was prepared. They have been -- the day before they have been at the site, burial site in Gornje Obrinje to make the excavations -- exhumations. Sorry. And when we want to go there to do the actual exhumations, we could not without having risked an armed incident, so we withdrew.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: I would like to call up exhibit P2820, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Mr. Kickert, that's a document dated 16th December 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object to the use of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: This document was disclosed to us yesterday evening at 1625. It had not been previously disclosed. It's in English and German. There's no complete English translation. There's no B/C/S translation for our clients. This document and this testimony indeed is not indicated in the 65 ter summary. For all those reasons we object for lack of notice and lack of inadequate time to prepare for this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Moeller.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Your Honours, it's correct that that document was disclosed yesterday.
