The reason is I had on the notification another document, Exhibit P2657, which had the same subject line as this document: Obstacles for the Finnish Forensic Expert Team," but which dealt with everything else but the Finnish forensic team. Now, when I talked to Mr. Kickert yesterday I inquired whether there was any document actually dealing with the issue of the Finnish forensic expert team, and this is the very document which I wasn't aware of previously. That's the reason why we disclosed it. I think the evidence that Mr. Kickert gave on that is admissible because it is dealt with in his statement. He refers in two paragraphs on page 5 of his statement to the work of the Finnish forensic team and the problems encountered and what was done about it. And we would tender this document only in support of his testimony on that point, basically on the note that you made recently that contemporaneous documents on the events are the best evidence we can present, and this is why we suggest this evidence now to be admitted, despite a relatively late notice of the document itself. As to the German and English, the content I want to rely on is only in the English text. Only the heading and maybe one sentence in the beginning is in German, which could be read out in English here, and then there is some four paragraphs at the end which are in German, but they deal with a different aspect, and we would -- we are of course working on translations as we speak about it. They hadn't been available this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Why had you not seek amendment of your Rule 65 ter list of exhibits?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I was -- I was planning to raise this issue later on, because I understand with the last witness where we had a lot of documents we sometimes filed -- had to file something in writing about the actual admission of documents. I would have addressed that then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In view of this failure to comply with the basic rule that we've invited you to follow, and indeed in view of the absence of just basic courtesy to the Trial Chamber, and also because of the late notification of this document for the reasons given by Mr. O'Sullivan, we refuse to allow you to tender this or to use it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I understand this ruling to mean that I may ask him some additional questions about the incident as such? May I, as --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It defeats me why you would bother with the document in view of what you had said earlier about the content of the witness's statement, and that has been disclosed, according to you. So -- I haven't seen the statement, as you know --

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- but I accept what you say about its contents, and that seems to answer Mr. O'Sullivan's point about the subject matter but not about the use of the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Mr. Kickert, on this -- the incident we just talked about, the aborted attempt to go to Gornje Obrinje that day, were there any further discussions about this incident later with the Serb authorities?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Yes, it was brought up, both in Belgrade and then as a matter of coincidence the Serb minister of justice --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, by your leave, I'm raising the issue of the basis for the questions put by my learned friend Ms. Moeller. The statement of the witness was not attached, only the documents were attached. Therefore, there is no basis for this incident, although my learned friend referred to the statement earlier on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Moeller.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: -- this is not a Rule 92 ter but a live witness, so we didn't put the statement on the notification, but the statement was disclosed yesterday as part of the witness 66(A)(ii) disclosure --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So the statement is not part of the 65 ter summary?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Of the summary, yes, but it is not an exhibit in e-court as P number, because we do not intend to tender the statement, as he is live.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So where is this referred to in the 65 ter summary, then?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the 65 ter summary is relatively short, which is why I put an additional notice to the Defence saying: "The Prosecution intends to lead evidence on all aspects dealt with in the witness statement dated 14 May--

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: -- and 8-9 June, which is one and the same --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: -- statement of five pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic, you'll see that there is reference to the statement in what is called "Additional Notice to the Defence."

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but the leave of the Chamber was not asked for in the meantime, as far as I know. And it is not contained in the original 65 ter list or in the summary, for that matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Moeller.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think, as I said, the witness summary is relatively generic in saying: "I was responsible for political issues focused on Kosovo," and we submit that is one aspect of it. And it is dealt with explicitly in the witness statement that we referred the Defence to, there cannot be a lack of notice, really, in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Why don't you follow the course that we instructed and ask for leave to amend these lists at the appropriate time? Why do you just ignore these rules that have been made?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Which -- amend the 65 ter summary, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, if you want to amend it, you need leave to do it. There was a deadline back in June for 65 ter lists, and you know that there is a rule requiring you to ask if you wish to amend it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: But, Your Honour, I -- what I was arguing is that it is actually included in the description of tasks and portfolio of the witness, as set out in the 65 ter summary. Now, if you're asking that each and every little detail of the statement goes into a 65 ter summary, that would blow these 65 ter summaries up very much. So that's why we often use more generic descriptions, and in this case I think it is covered by the description of what the witness will testify about in general terms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Direct my attention, please, to the description that includes this.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Well, the second sentence saying: "The witness was responsible for political issues and was focussed on Kosovo."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We will allow you to follow this line of examination in the way that -- the restricted way that can be done without the document, but that should not be understood as in any way accepting the submission you have just made to us. If you're right that notice is given in the second sentence of your 65 ter summary, then it is incomprehensible that you would add an additional notice to this. You obviously think that that doesn't -- or when it was drafted didn't cover the various matters that were referred to in the statement. And therefore, to make the position clear you've added this additional notice to the Defence. And it really isn't acceptable to suggest that that second sentence would be adequate notice of evidence about the obstructive behaviour of Serb authorities in relation to exhumations, if that's what you're leading evidence about. So please don't treat the Bench as having no understanding of what the content of a 65 ter summary ought to have. But as far as this issue is concerned, we will allow you to pursue it in this way by asking further questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And I apologise if I offended you. I only put this additional notice to indicate that this was our interpretation of the 65 ter summary, but I take your point, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Mr. Kickert, just a few more questions on this issue.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm seeing --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: One moment. Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may I be allowed to go back to this issue again. I may be mistaken, but I don't think at any point in the statement there is anything mentioning exhumations, and my learned friend may correct me if I'm wrong. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we have the disadvantage of not having the statement, so I am relying on what I'm being told.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I refer you to the statement?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, just tell me what it says.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: It says that the witness had dealings with Zoran Andjelkovic when he worked to facilitate access for the Finnish forensic team and that he also met with the Serbian minister of justice after access to the site at Gornje Obrinje was denied to the Finnish forensic team. Now, access to a site, yes, I think that -- what would the Finnish forensic team do at the site but exhumations, even if the word "exhumations" is not in the statement, I submit that is notice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah. Mr. Cepic, we already had reference to the fact that this was to do with exhumations and there was no objection taken at that stage. We don't want to go back to this and we will allow Ms. Moeller to continue, as we've already stipulated.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Mr. Kickert, once the attempt to go to the site at Gornje Obrinje was aborted, was this discussed with the Serbian authorities?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Yes. When I -- my last intervention, the Serbian Minister of Justice happened to be in Pristina that day and we were able to meet him in the government building in Pristina, and I brought that forward, that issue. And also what I saw as a breach of the Vienna Diplomatic Convention as a -- a photograph of -- not a photograph but the apparatus, the photo apparatus -- the camera of Mr. Timo Lehelma, the Finnish ambassador accompanying the team was taken away while sitting in a diplomatic vehicle. And so we brought also this issue up with the Serbian Minister of Justice and later on also in Belgrade, but it was to no avail. The Finnish forensic team did not start exhumations in Gornje Obrinje before the Christmas break. They left home and from the 1st of January, 1999, I was no longer responsible, because I was no longer EU Presidency but it was the Germans.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I would like to move on to Exhibit P560, please. That's a document from 7 October 1998. It says at the top "Special Report Kickert," so is it correct to conclude --

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: -- you were the author?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: SB is not --

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: SB --

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: It's [German spoken]. It's [German spoken], but it's just author Kickert.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Author. Okay. You authored that document, right?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: It refers to a meeting, I think, of Ambassador Petritsch with Mr. Sainovic. Were you present at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: I would like you to look at the second sentence in the first paragraph which says that "Sainovic is considered a close associate of Yugoslav President Milosevic and is thought to be responsible for coordinating the security forces in Kosovo since the summer." What was the information upon you - you meaning again you and the Austrian Embassy - included this in your report?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Well, this was our assessment of his role all along summer. Mr. Sainovic was very often down in Pristina in the government building, and we know that at one occasion for sure that Ambassador -- the US Ambassador Chris Hill met him there in Pristina in the government building, and he was referred to us as the person the Americans would bring security issues up with. For us, the meeting on 7th of October was the very first meeting that we had with Mr. Sainovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And did you learn at any time any information which would indicate that the statement in this report about Mr. Sainovic's role would have been wrong, would have been different?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: We were not discussing security issues as such, hard-core security issues with Mr. Sainovic. So I could neither one way or the other -- it is our assessment we got -- our impression we got from hearing that he was an interlocutor for security issues for the Americans.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And why was it that meetings on security issues were held more or less by the Americans?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Well, you have to understand that the EU had not a common foreign security policy at that time, and actually Ambassador Petritsch was -- was the real first special envoy named, and actually, at this very time he was already in his new position, an agreement in principle to name him EU Special Envoy in Kosovo was made at the General Affairs Council meeting, the informal one, at the margins at the General Assembly in New York about September and officially he was formalised as EU Special Envoy, if I'm not mistaken, at the General Affairs Council on the 5th of October. So it was just after he was named that Mr. Sainovic was ready to see Ambassador Petritsch. We had generally also as EU Presidency problems of access. I put it very bluntly. We were as EU a soft power, not taken seriously and certainly not on par with the Americans.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Was there any reference from the Yugoslav side who they would rather have as interlocutors, the EU or the US?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: No. The main dealings were with Americans, general. Also on -- by this time there were already with what we called the Hill drafts, sort of drafts for an interim agreement, political agreement, were circulating and given to one side and the other side. It was always the Americans who would discuss these drafts with the Serb interlocutors. It was not us, it was not the EU.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us a little bit more about this meeting with Mr. Sainovic on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: I think it says pretty much all. I think the most important is what all the meetings in the end of September/beginning of October stated that it was announced that the -- that the offensive or the action of the security forces have ended. And I think it had to do also with the deadline of Security Council Resolution 1199.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And the bullet point referring to this issue, I think it's the third from the bottom in the English version: "Action by security forces was allegedly called off on 28 September. Since then, no serious clashes." The sentence after that: "Were it possible to accept the argument of the US ..." Can you explain that. It's not quite clear to me what this is meant to say.

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Well, I'm reading it in German and -- well, it says that he could accept that the fights have ended just -- maybe just five days ago. It's just impossible that actions would stop from one moment to the other and withdraw security forces. So even if you set a target date of 28 - that's my interpretation now - of 28 of September, you -- by retreating your security forces, you could not stop -- avoid certain fights once and for all on this target date.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Did you have any other independent information on what the situation was during these days, the last days in September in terms of the ending of the operations?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: There was a report by ECMM which was also shared with the UN to be a basis for the Secretary-General's report based on Security Council Resolution 1199. So there must be a report submitted to New York by us, by the ECMM.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And the last exhibit I would like to look at with you is Exhibit P562.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: If we could go to the last page first, please, the third page.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: This is an e-mail dispatch from the 20th of February, 1999, and your name, Mr. Kickert, appears at the end of the text, Petritsch/Kickert.

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: But on the first page as SB, author, is a Mr. Senfter --

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: He --

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: -- could you explain how this report came together.

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: This is a report I filed from the castle of Rambouillet, and it was a little complicated, but I had a ciphering device which I used in Kosovo, which deciphering device was in Belgrade. So for that matter I sent this report to Belgrade and then my colleague, Mr. Senfter, would forward it to Vienna.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We saw a number of these communications earlier with Mr. Petritsch, and these ones tend to bear a time as well as a date. And some of them bear odd times like 3.00 in the morning, for example. Did you have a practice during these negotiations of communicating quickly or is it just coincidental that these times appear on the telegram?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. It was our intention to have, if possible, same-day reporting, meaning reporting every day. At times, the -- I was not available to find time to write but in the night, and that's when I filed them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Moeller.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Could we now have a look at page 2, please. The third-last paragraph from the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: It refers to lengthy talks held with the undersigned and President Milutinovic.

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Yeah, this refers to Ambassador Petritsch.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes. Were you, Mr. Kickert, present at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Not to my knowledge. This paragraph must have been inserted by Ambassador Petritsch. So when we wrote reports, I would do the general report and he would either make changes or add something. And this paragraph must have been added by him.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Now, more generally to Rambouillet, you already mentioned you were there. And what was your role at Rambouillet?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: I was Mr. Petritsch's assistant and sort of -- I did the reporting; and as my job in general was more liaising with the Kosovo Albanians, I did the same also in Rambouillet.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kickert.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Your Honours, that concludes my direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, we'll follow the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Just give me a moment. Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I believe you still have the documents that the Prosecutor gave you in front of you.

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Can I ask you to find P564. P564. I'm just waiting for it to come up on the screen for others. All right. P564 is a document dated the 11th September 1998. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And you composed that document?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And Ambassador Petritsch signed it?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And I believe you told us that often you would prepare documents and Ambassador Petritsch would review it and approve it; correct?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Were there times, however, where you would compose a document by yourself and it wouldn't be reviewed by Ambassador Petritsch. You just said you would send it off --

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: We have strict rules in our service. So if I would sent it off, that nobody had seen it or approved of it, it would be my name at the bottom of a report.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: But at this trip, Ambassador Petritsch was not present, so he would have just looked at it and said, Send it.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: So two sets of eyes look at it to see its accuracy?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Well, I mean, as he was not present, he would not be able to write anything on the substance.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Okay. Let's look at the third bullet point. This says: "Junik has been little damaged." And then the next sentence was: "However there is nothing to be seen of the 1.000 people who have returned home from the Serbian side." Do you see that sentence?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And today, during your testimony, you offered this interpretation. You said: "I don't think that Junik had any Serbian -- any major Serbian population, so it must have been Albanian. So my interpretation now is that they claimed that a thousand people had returned and I -- I state there that I haven't seen many people, certainly not a thousand people." So it appears that something slipped into this report that wasn't quite accurate?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Yeah, from time to time it happened that I was writing quickly and you would find sentences not finished. And from my point of view now, I may be mistaken, but this is how I interpret it now. This isn't a sentence which makes sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Let's turn to a different topic. You were talking about an Exhibit -- P558 is the next one. P558. Do you have the hard copy, sir?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is it 2558? It's not simply 558.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: That's my mistake. P558.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Right. "28 September, 1998." Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And that's where you -- we've seen that you made the correction that the word "assessment" instead of "verdict" is a mistranslation and "cover-up" should be "alibi operation." In this context you said that you had visited Djakovica early in the month of September 1998; correct?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: This is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And that visit in -- at the beginning of September was, again, in connection to the creation of local police forces; right?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: This is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: In other words, Albanian -- people of Albanian ethnicity making up the security force; correct?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And the object of this exercise was to, as I believe you've said, create trust and confidence within the community or the communities that were living there; correct?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Yes, so that they would feel more secure and return.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And you see here that your British colleague told you that in fact there were people at that time in -- at the end of September 1998, that's P558, there were people in the office in uniform with insignia and that there was a plan to have them receive hand-guns; correct?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: So it would appear that some steps had been taken in that direction to at least begin to create this local force with Albanian people in it?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Force -- or as they were called, security coordinators.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Right. And also the -- this afternoon you told us that events overtook the situation shortly thereafter with the Holbrooke-Milosevic Agreement and therefore this sort of faded away, this initiative; correct?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: This is my understanding, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I've obviously misunderstood this earlier. I thought the reference to them already wearing uniforms with insignia was to what your colleague had been told, but is that actually a reflection of what he had seen in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's what he had seen. He hasn't seen them wearing side-arms because it was announced that they would get these side-arms and ammunition the very next day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, but you then later on your own visit don't actually see any of them.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was previous. My visit --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ah.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- was previous to this one. And at that time it was still some insecurity by the deputy of Djakovica whether they would wear uniforms or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification. I had misunderstood.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And perhaps in line with His Honour's question, we can look at P559 --

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: -- which you don't have in hard copy but which will appear on the screen, P559. I think you have it now. It's a document dated September 7th, 1998.

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And that gives an account of the visit we were discussing earlier in September; correct?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And I want to draw your attention to the last paragraph, if you can just have a look at it, and I can ask you some questions about that. You see what you highlight in your concluding paragraph is -- are the inherent problems or risks associated with this. On the one hand, the Serbs would be giving ethnic Albanians weapons; on the other hand, the ethnic Albanians who agreed to participate in this local force could be seen as traitors?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And you say could be subject to UCK persecution?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: So it was a very difficult situation, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I'd like to change topics for a second. In your testimony you mentioned some of the first contacts you had with the KLA, but you said that previous to that, the Americans, and particularly Mr. Holbrooke, had contact with the KLA. And I'm looking at the transcript and you said there was one time when Mr. Holbrooke was in Junik where there were even pictures of him with the KLA. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Those are -- the pictures I'm thinking of are the ones that made it into the television and print media where we see Mr. Holbrooke and I believe Ambassador Hill at an Albanian home in the traditional way with their shoes off and sitting along the wall and a man with a beard and a KLA uniform carrying a Kalashnikov moves in and sits down right beside Mr. Holbrooke. Is that what we're talking about?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: That's the picture I have in mind, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And you also say that -- this morning you've told us that there were contacts between the Americans and the KLA on other levels.

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Do you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Yes, I believe it was on military attache level or outside of Kosovo itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, let's call up Exhibit 5D121, 5D121.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: 5D121 is dated 27 June, 1998. You see your name at the top right-hand corner --

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Could I have the German version, please, because my trust of the translations is ...

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I'm not sure -- well, I'm not sure if we have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Do we have it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry, no German today. You'll have to make use of this one.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It takes away some of the authenticity of it but I'll give it a try.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Let's talk about the contents of it. You see on that first page, point number 1, "State of the US and RF," Russian Federation, "initiatives." Do you see that; correct?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: No. My screen: "Contact Group, Head of Mission Meeting 27th of June."

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: You've got the document 27 June, 1998 in front of you?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The one in front of me is a German version.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, that's the former report of the local police at the left-hand side. So that's -- we went past this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Indeed, that's Vienna --

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I'm referring to the document dated 27 June, 1998, that's 5D121, and it says: "Austrian Embassy Sarajevo - please forward ASAP."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's on my screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And it gives an account of a two-hour meeting between the Contact Group, head of missions, here, and the OSCE. "German in office held today 27 June under German chairmanship and attended for the first time by the undersigned," who is Ambassador Petritsch. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Then there is point number 1: "State of the US and RF initiatives." Okay?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And the third bullet point is the American -- Americans informing this -- people at this meeting -- they're playing down the contact between Holbrooke and the UCK saying it's fortuitous. "No political talks, only humanitarian and supply issues discussed. A man in UCK uniform forced his way into the picture." That's what we just talked about.

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: The next bullet point, which you've actually mentioned a moment ago. "On the other hand, by their own admission, there have long been contacts with UCK representatives at the US military attache level." Could you explain that and tell us what you know about that, what you heard?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: This was mentioned in that meeting; otherwise, I would not have written it down there.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Correct. And what did you -- what details did you know about it then or learn about in your work in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: For us it was sort of the first admittance of these contacts on that level because until then our policy was to avoid contacts with the UCK and, for example, the British colleague I've talked about earlier, he did not have authority to meet KLA until later in July.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, what were -- what would the contacts have been? What was your knowledge of the contacts between the KLA and the US military?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: No knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: All right. A moment ago you also mentioned that you heard about or you knew about contacts between the KLA and the Americans outside of the FRY. What do you know about that? What can you tell us about that?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Well, the KLA had representatives abroad, mainly in Geneva and there too it was the Americans who had contacts with them first, before we had.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: This would be, again, on the military level?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: No, that would be the political level.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Do you know which individuals on the American side?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: I imagine that it was Mr. Larry Rossin who was responsible for southeast Europe and the state department.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Do you know who he met on the KLA side?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: I suspect it was Badima Mahmuti.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: What was he in the KLA?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: He presented himself as a spokesperson abroad of the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: All right. In hard copy I believe you have Exhibit P562, that's the last document you looked at.

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Just for the transcript I believe you said that Larry Rossin was responsible for south-east Europe at the US State Department, is that right?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And his name is spelled -- do you know how to spell his name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: R-o-s-s-i-n.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Thank you. All right. You have P562 in front of you and we have it on the screen. It's the document dated 20 February 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Now, my friend the Prosecutor directed you to -- on the second page, the third-last paragraph. The second page, third-last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Petritsch testified here a couple of days ago and he said he -- that you composed this document and he never said that he inserted this paragraph. Now, what do you say to that?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Well, I mean, I can't recall that I was present at that meeting, so I could not have written it.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: But he said you wrote it. What do you say to that?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: I wrote the report as such --

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Your Honour, objection --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But as I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Hold on, please, Mr. Kickert. Mr. --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But as I said earlier --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, no, please, please just a moment. Thank you. Ms. --

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: I recall Mr. Petritsch testifying that Mr. Kickert drafted the documents and he revised it and sometimes shortened them or put something in. That's what Mr. Petritsch testified, to my memory, and I don't think he was explicitly asked whether Mr. Kickert drafted this particular paragraph and said yes, that did not happen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think there's a mistake in the transcript here. I think you said you recalled Petritsch saying he -- is that right?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. I don't know whether I misspoke --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You better go through that --

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Shall I repeat that, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No. Just hold on a second -- so are you disputing Mr. O'Sullivan's contention that Mr. Petritsch said that Mr. Kickert composed the document?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes. My argument is that he only tells Mr. Kickert half of what Mr. Petritsch said and he does not tell Mr. Kickert that Mr. Petritsch also said that he revised this document and he would shorten such documents sometimes and sometimes add to them. And the second point is Mr. Petritsch was not asked explicitly whether Mr. Kickert drafted this particular paragraph and he did not answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Have you a page reference for this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The date is --

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: -- The 2nd of March, line 22. I can read it for the Court. Ambassador Petritsch says: "P --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just a second until we see it. 10 -- sorry --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The words are: "That was written by Mr. Kickert."

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: But it also says: "Usually that happens that there is a draft and then I go" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just, I think we've heard enough. This is another of these objections that really is quite inappropriate, because it's a matter of exploration in evidence what actually happened. You will have your chance in re-examination to clarify this. The point's probably been completely lost now because this debate has taken place in front of the witness. So please don't interrupt when it's clearly a matter of dispute and it can be resolved so far as you're concerned by re-examination. I don't accept your submission that there was a misrepresentation of the evidence of Mr. Petritsch. Mr. O'Sullivan, it's back to you. Take it up in whatever way you think is appropriate.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, I think I'll just leave the point now because of what you just said and I hope it's left by the other side as well on that same basis. Let's go to the first page of this document --

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, first of all, the first page. You see the date is 20 February 1999, 0600 hours.

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And in his testimony, Ambassador Petritsch at page 10884 said that it had been prepared -- this document had been prepared by you just before sending it, just before 0600 hours in the morning. In fact, you had been working on it during the night. Does that sound right?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Must have been.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Okay. Now, the -- on the first page we see an entry there that talks about the afternoon of the 19th of February where Ambassador Petritsch has been working with the Kosovars on a re-drafting of the Rambouillet Agreement. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: If -- I'm just -- sorry, I'm just --

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I'll read the sentence to you --

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: No, before I get there. This 6 hours is up at the --

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: -- at what the embassy in Belgrade put on. And then my remark is in quotation marks starting from 19th of February all the way down, talk about 19th of February. So it doesn't -- so as long as the quotation marks, it doesn't say when it was sent by me to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Do you have any reason to dispute what Mr. Petritsch said about that, what I just read to you?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: No. I'm just wondering why 6.00 in the morning why is it on top and not within the quotation mark of the report, "Our embassy had sent on to Vienna."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand what you're saying but if you look at the heading, certainly in the English version it seems to be saying: "This is the situation at the Rambouillet negotiations" --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 6.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- "at 6.00." So it doesn't seem to refer to the time at which Belgrade was sending on the telegram to Vienna.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: So the second paragraph of that first page it says: "On the afternoon of 19th February, the Kosovars put forward concrete drafting proposals" --

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Redrafting proposals.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Redrafting proposals for the key pass -- for the passages of key concern to them --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the speakers please make significantly longer pauses between question and answer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... do you recall him meeting that afternoon with the Kosovar delegation?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: I was probably present. I was normally present if there were meetings with the bigger delegations -- the whole delegations. Meetings where the -- where the three negotiators had on smaller scale, I was rarely present. So on this one I was probably present because it looked like an official bigger gathering.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Okay. Then we go to the second page and second page gives accounts of certain things that happened on the evening of the 19th of February, which is, I can tell you, a Friday. All right. I can make that representation to you. And the top of page 2, first several paragraphs, refer to meetings between members of the Kosovar delegation and NATO. You might recall those are the meetings held with General Clark; correct?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: I would not be able to confirm that. I can't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Okay. Then you go down to the third paragraph --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. O'Sullivan, there is some difficulty over the speed of this interchange. If you can just please bear in mind the need to pause.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Then the third paragraph, again in the evening, we see the first part of that third paragraph says that Mr. Cook, Mr. Petritsch, and Ambassador Mayorski had meetings on further procedure; correct?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And then that was followed by talks with selected Kosovars in order to encourage them to accept the texts; correct?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Then the next paragraph deals with a meeting between Mr. Hill, Mr. Petritsch, and Mr. Thaqi. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: "On the evening of the 19th," second half of the paragraph, do you see that?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Do you recall that Thaqi had been in Ljubljana that day to see Demaqi?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And Hill had gone to Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: So this would have been late in the evening I would assume that this meeting took place?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Then there's the meeting with Mr. Milutinovic, Ambassadors Petritsch and Mayorski, and there's no indication of what time of day that took place; right?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: On the timing, but it took place on the 19th of February.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Okay. Then the paragraph below that talks about a provisional timetable for the 20th of February, and you may recall the 20th of February is the second -- it's the second Saturday of Rambouillet. That's the day that the Contact Group foreign ministers met individually with each delegation. Do you recall that taking place? It was supposed to be the final day of Rambouillet.

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Right. I mean, I remember that -- all the Contact Group foreign ministers had arrived apparently on this day.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: You may recall that Rambouillet was extended three extra days after this 20th; correct?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And you see there's a provisional timetable. So CG 7.30, Contact Group meeting at the PS level, that would that mean?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: PD, in German, political directors' level.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Okay. And then at 8.00 in the morning is when the first ministers arrive and each delegation will come in to see them -- appear before the Contact Group foreign ministers; correct?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Yes, they would arrive and then there were bilateral meetings with the delegations --

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Right --

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: -- or with single of their members.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Right. So if you go -- if you put your mind back to the 19th and 20th, we're at a point where the conference could be ending on the 20th, the next day, we don't know if there's going to be an extension. And we have all this activity the night before. We have, as I suggested to you, the Albanians are seeing Clark, your Ambassador is meeting with Mr. Cook and Mr. Mayorski, with the Kosovar delegation. Then Mr. Petritsch is meeting with Mr. Hill and Demaqi --

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: No, not Demaqi, Thaqi.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Thaqi. Excuse me. Thaqi. And your recollection is that you were working on the creation of this document overnight so it could give a snap-shot of what happened by 6.00 in the morning on the 20th; right?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let's look at the next paragraph. It says: "During the morning there was a rapprochement of the views on the political parts."

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: So obviously -- well, keep going. "Most important outstanding part now is Yug's agreement to the Implementation Annexes," it should say above all, "stationing of NATO troops). Hill and the undersigned -- that's Petritsch -- agree that the deadline should perhaps be extended two to three days at the most but only if the Yugoslav side unambiguously confirms its acceptance of the presence of international troops." So this meeting that you've described here took place before the 6.00 in the morning, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Yeah. I mean, now that you tell me that it was the last night before the Contact Group foreign ministers came, there was discussions. I remember that the -- Jim O'Brien and the lawyers went up to see the Serb delegation in their rooms the whole night and I remember that with Ambassador Hill we met in the early-morning hours with the Kosovo Albanian delegation.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: So we're talking about a pretty hectic, highly charged night, aren't we?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: We're talking about an intense night.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do have some questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Kickert. My name is Toma Fila. I'm representing Mr. Sainovic. I will be questioning you about document P560.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could it please be brought to the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: It is the telegram that Ms. Moeller has been questioned you extensively. Before I move on to this question, we received from the Prosecution, on the 6th of March, your supplemental statement. I don't know whether this supplemental statement has been shown to you by the Prosecution, but in relation to P560, that is the dispatch drafted by you and Mr. Petritsch, either separately or together, it says here, in relation to P560, Kickert was present at the meeting with Sainovic. This meeting was something like a business meeting. And now, totally unrelated to the telegram itself, you say the following: "Sainovic, in 1998, flew regularly to Pristina and Chris Hill would meet him there in the government building in Pristina. The European Community was not the chief interlocutor. Serbs prefer to speak to the Americans," and so on and so forth. Mr. Kickert, what I want to know is: What does this sentence: "Mr. Sainovic flew regularly to Pristina to meet Mr. Hill," what does it have to do with the telegram? Why did you say this if you, in fact, did say this? If I have not been clear, I will repeat. In the telegram that you write, you do not mention Chris Hill nor Mr. Sainovic flying to Pristina, you do not mention any talks of anything. How can that you mention Chris Hill in relation to telegram 560 since Ms. Moeller did not explain to us how God worked in mysterious ways to bring us to this point. This is what I wanted to ask you.

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: This is the explanation why at the beginning before I cite that Mr. Sainovic told Mr. Petritsch at that meeting on the 7th of October how I describe Mr. Sainovic in our assessment. And it only came that Mr. Hill came into this because we knew from Mr. Hill that he met Mr. Sainovic in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Fine. Fine. And based on this you draw this conclusion that because Mr. Hill was in charge of security that Sainovic spoke to him about this area. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Hill was regularly debriefing us of his talks he had with Serb interlocutors and he also told us about meetings he had and at least one, if not more, with Mr. Sainovic in the government building in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Fine. I understand you here. Mr. Petritsch, when he testified here a couple of days ago, he was shown by a different Prosecutor the same sentence that we just spoke about. And on that occasion, Mr. Petritsch said, that's page 10767, lines 14 and above, that this sentence was put in here because he had read something like that in the papers or there had been a press release by the Yugoslav government. And because his memory was not quite clear and he wasn't really sure about that, he added the sentence: "Our understanding in the diplomatic circles was that Mr. Sainovic was in charge of Kosovo," without specifying the part of Kosovo. How would you comment on this statement made by Mr. Petritsch? He did not mention Mr. Hill or anything like this. He provided a totally different explanation, in other words.

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: I just answered on a question posed to me on the best of my recollection. And I'm not -- I cannot comment on Mr. Petritsch, what his motivation was to answer differently.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Fine, fine. And the dispatch that was sent is, in fact, a work both by you and Mr. Petritsch because, as far as I can see, as far as I know, it is Mr. Petritsch who signed the dispatch and he is responsible for the contents, is that correct, not you?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Yes, I wrote it and --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. But he signed it?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: He signed it off, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: That's correct. Yes. You will agree with me that you did not attend the meetings, one meeting or several meetings between Mr. Hill and Sainovic in Pristina. And you have no idea what they spoke about. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: I did not attend a meeting between Mr. Hill and Mr. Sainovic in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Do you know that Mr. Hill was in fact the chief political representative of the USA in all the negotiations with Serbia, both in Pristina and in Belgrade and, in fact, also in Rambouillet? Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: That is true, but he also had people with him at meetings like Mr. Burns from the US KDOM who indeed dealt with security matters and who signed agreements in October on where Serb police had to withdraw or where they could drive back and forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Mr. Petritsch, in his evidence, told us that in a critical night that you yourself spoke about that Mr. Hill appeared with a demand that the word "referendum after three years" be put in the agreement. That's what Mr. Petritsch said. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: I think that the word "referendum" was avoided. To my knowledge, it was taking account of the will of the people --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Later on, yes.

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: -- to avoid the word "referendum."

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So I fully agree with what you say but what I said is also true. You say -- you spoke about the end and I spoke about the beginning. At the beginning, Mr. Hill appeared demanding that the words "referendum after three years" to be put in, and Mr. Petritsch objected and so did the European Community and that's why the word was not put in. But Mr. Hill used the word "referendum." Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: I don't know whether Mr. Hill used the word referendum but that was certainly what the Kosovo Albanians wanted to have included and we wanted to have it balanced and not have the word "referendum" in there.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Let me just check something here. And finally, could you please tell me one more thing. You used the following wording. The meeting that you attended was like a business meeting before saying that he went to see Hill in Pristina. What do you mean when you say a "business meeting" because this word is not there in the telegram. What did you mean by that? Just to cut a long story short, did you want it to say that they did not discuss any issues related to security but that this was a political discussion?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: We never discussed security, neither in Rambouillet nor before. We were diplomats. We are from a neutral country, so this was not a subject we were dealt with. Business-like meeting was probably because it was the first meeting of the two of them and there was sort of no particular demands. But it was for the two of them to meet first time, get to know each other, and build on this for future meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Mr. Petritsch later said that they had many meetings, I don't know how many of those meetings you yourself attended, and he characterised Sainovic as a highly cooperative person who wanted peace, who advocated peace at Rambouillet. But he said that somebody else unfortunately had prevented that later. Do you agree with what Mr. Petritsch had said?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: We certainly dealt very well with Mr. Sainovic. He's a person, I would describe, you could do business with and who you never had sort of acrimonious fights on anything but was somebody you could really talk things through with.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Well, otherwise it would appear that the only thing he did was to make sure that you had electricity for two days. Thank you very much. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic -- Mr. Sepenuk, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: No questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Aleksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Just a few questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Kickert. My name is Djuro Cepic. I'm on the Defence team representing General Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to ask the registrar to show Defence Exhibit 5D119, to bring it on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kickert, it seems that, unfortunately -- no -- okay. We have it both in German and in English. Excellent. This is a report of the 24th of July, 1998, and here at the top right-hand corner you see that it says "desk officer Kickert." Did you, yourself, draft this report?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please scroll down a little bit. Fine. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: And here at the bottom of the page it says: "The meeting on the 23rd of July in Malisevo," and then it says below that it was held in the presence of Gani Krasniqi, one of the KLA commanders, and his position in the chain of command is described. Did you, yourself, attend this meeting with Mr. Krasniqi?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Yeah, that report, that particular report, is the follow-on meeting I had where I met with number 3 which was Hashim Thaqi and I also attended a meeting, and that must have been the previous day where the secretary-general Albert Rohan was going to Malisevo and where he met with number 7 and Gani Krasniqi, and I was present at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And after this date, did you have any other meetings with the KLA in Malisevo?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: As I said, the first meeting was just with number 7 and the next day with number 3 and 7. That was a meeting I was having alone with no other interlocutor from the Austrian Embassy or Austrian foreign ministry, just accompanied by Kosovo Albanian journalist who facilitated the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Is the name of this journalist Baton Haxhiu?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Baton Haxhiu was present at the meeting with number 7 but he did not facilitate the meeting. The meeting was organised by ECMM. The meeting I had with number 3 was facilitated by another journalist Dukagjin Gorani also from Koha Ditore. Mr. Baton Haxhiu was facilitating a follow-on meeting which my British colleague, David Slinn, and I had in Klecka with Jakup Krasniqi, Ram Buja, and Fatmir Limaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You do know that at that time some crimes were committed in Klecka; right?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: That was the allegation. That's why we also put it on the list of those sites which the Finnish forensic experts should have looked into.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The catalogue you've just given of meetings there with KLA representatives isn't terribly clear, I think, from the transcript. Did you have only two meetings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I -- in July, I had three meetings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Three. And it was the first one with someone you know only as number 7?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I know his proper name now, it's Kadri Veseli.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And then the middle meeting must be the one at which Krasniqi was present. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'll try to clarify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Was he also present at the third one with Thaqi, is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Mr. Gani Krasniqi was present at the very first meeting which must have taken place on the 22nd of July when the Secretary-General was visiting, coming down from Belgrade and we went with ECMM to Malisevo. Then we met number 7, Kadri Veseli. The very next day I was going on my own. Mr. Rohan was already returning to Belgrade. Through this Kosovar journalist, I was able to meet number 3, Mr. Hashim Thaqi on the 23rd of July. And later that month, after Malisevo was abandoned and we still wanted to keep in touch with the KLA to include them in the political process, I went to Klecka but met other people there. As I said, Jakup Krasniqi, the internal spokesperson of the KLA, I met there also Ram Buja and Fatmir Limaj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kickert. Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Well, we mentioned Mr. Baton Haxhiu and you said that he facilitated the meeting in Klecka with Limaj, Krasniqi, and Buja. Mr. Haxhiu was on excellent terms with the KLA top; right?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: He was always able to report on the KLA in the newspaper and he was in contact with them and he was able to facilitate our meetings with the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see page 3 of this document that I had brought on the screen, if we could see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kickert, you mentioned Orahovac and the KLA attack on Orahovac, and here in the first few sentences here we can see a report by a journalist Enver Maloku, and then in line 4 it says here that he was recently a victim of a mysterious assassination attempt. So he was not as fortunate as Mr. Haxhiu to be able to publish everything about the KLA. Could you please comment on these allegations here about how hundreds of civilians were killed and the assassination attempt on Mr. Maloku. So the first four sentences that all relate to Orahovac. [In English] "In article by Enver Maloku, leader of Kosovo information centre of the LDK, in which he accused the KLA of irresponsible behaviour in Orahovac which took the lives of hundreds of civilians, also contributed to increasing the fractured relationship between the KLA and the LDK."

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: The LDK.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: "Maloku was recently the victim of the mysterious assassination attempt".

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: That's a correct translation. The LDK, for the longest time, including Mr. Rugova, denied the existence of the UCK and there, in this article, when I wrote it down, it was certainly information of the Kosovo Information Centre which I referred to earlier as -- with their daily informations trying to put their side of the picture to the public and I cite that. And it was sort of our -- our attempt to get to grips with this organisation where we really didn't know how it was structured and who our potential interlocutors could be to integrate them in the political process. And apparently, I write that there seems to be fractions within the UCK. I refer to a central command in Malisevo and -- and that they're trying to bring them in line.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you perhaps have any knowledge who actually attempted to assassinate Mr. Maloku? Did you perhaps learn of that later on? Do you recall that, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: No idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Now, when you mentioned the central command in Malisevo, do you know, do you perhaps remember that the central command in fact ordered the villagers of Malisevo to leave or the inhabitants of Malisevo to leave the town together with them?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: I don't know about it, but I would not be surprised.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: That was, in fact, frequently the practice of the KLA to order the civilians to leave a certain area together with them; right?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: I cannot say whether they were ordered or whether they left because they felt insecure without them.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned the visit by Madam Emma Bonino, that's page 69 of the transcript, the visit to the Drenica and Malisevo areas. And you mentioned that the KLA did not allow you to enter their area because of the large number of media representatives that were together with you. Do you perhaps know why they did not allow you to enter into their zone, the real reason why they didn't allow you to go in?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: I cannot say more than the fact that they didn't let us in. That's all I can say. I have no idea what the reasoning was; nobody told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kickert. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cepic. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have a few questions for Mr. Kickert.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Kickert.

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My name is Branko Lukic, and I will have a couple of questions for you -- in fact, I will be just asking you to clarify things to help us understand. In Prosecution exhibit that was shown first, that would be P2666, the location of Baboloc is mentioned and the document indicates that this is a location for refugees, a refugee centre, for refugees of Slovenian background, Slavic background.

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: It says in German of Slavic background and I don't know where I got the information from that they are from Albania. But, at any rate, they -- we communicated in Serbian with them and I remember that at the early days of ECMM, where we also had colleagues of the foreign ministry in ECMM and we had just one team, they were assaulted physically by the people in Baboloc when they went there. That's why I refer that there were a lot of frictions there because they felt very insecure in this area where we had a lot of UCK activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And then one paragraph down it says, "Information Meeting Between the Foreign Minister and the Interior Minister of Yugoslavia." And in item 1 it says, "police actions are response to murders and abductions of police officers particularly to the attempts by terrorist gangs to block the main route." In relation to this, I would like to ask you if you had any personal experience where the KLA actually attempted to block the roads in Kosovo and do you know if they were successful doing that?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: There were times where we passed KLA check-points. For example, that meeting we had in Malisevo, the first one we passed a KLA check-point just on the outskirts of Suva Reka. Then I referred to earlier that at times we were denied passage by the KLA check-points. This happened. This happened both sides. There's nothing, just black and white -- yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And in relation to this, you told us that in July you travelled down the Pristina-Pec road and that you were stopped by the police and that they would not let you through. And only after you mentioned Odalovic's name was -- were you allowed to pass. What I want to ask you is can you remember -- can you perhaps be more specific about the date and the location of this incident?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: It was with the political directors troika of the EU. That must have been end of July. It was not the big check-point at Komorane juncture. It must have been somewhere before or after because this is then when we went to Pec road and then I think we went south to Malisevo or we attempted to go south. So somewhere on this road, but I cannot tell by certainty. But having the picture of the Komorane check-point in my mind, I don't think it was Komorane but somewhere else.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Okay. [Interpretation] Thank you. Do you remember, since as you said yourself this was towards the end of July, when there was intensive fighting going on between the Serb forces and the KLA, what you were told was the reason they were not allowing you to go any further? Were you stopped because of the security situation for your own security and safety and that of your mission?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: The reasons they gave us was they had orders not to let anybody through. They did not get to -- as good policemen, they did not get into a discussion, but they just said, I have the order. And when they radioed back, eventually they waited there for half an hour, I don't know, three-quarters of an hour. They eventually let us through.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When asked by the Prosecutor, you explained that Malisevo was the capital of the KLA. Did you mean by that that for them it was the capital of Kosovo, the Republic of Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: No. The way portrayed it, it was sort of their intermestic [phoen] capital of what they called "the free areas" where the Serb police had no access.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember that before Malisevo the KLA had set up roadblocks from every direction and they controlled all traffic going in and out?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: As I said earlier, the very first time I went into the field was this organised trip on the 8th of June. And before I didn't go into the field. So there I cannot say what really happened. Whether I remember that this road was blocked and I remember also that Mr. Holbrooke said Kijevo, where there was a Serbian and to my knowledge also a Roma population, was the most dangerous place on earth at a certain period because it was isolated. There was no communication lines to this place.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you aware that in the Malisevo area, even after the KLA withdrew, there was frequent fighting between the KLA and the Serb security forces?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: There was fighting going on in the area -- in the greater Drenica area all through summer with -- until the KVM came and deployed and it was quieter, but then also at the end of the year of 1998, there were again skirmishes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I asked you about Malisevo, but as you saw more and more destruction going on, our Defence is putting it to you that in Malisevo there was continuous fighting between the KLA and Serb forces, that there was -- there were constant hostilities. And would you accept that as the main reason for all the fires and destruction of buildings?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: No. A building cannot be torn down by occasional fire-fights. I mean, shooting with guns cannot bring a house to collapse.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You are not a military expert, but we have heard here from other witnesses that incendiary bullets can set fire to a house. However, I will move on to another topic. In Exhibit P2655 -- I do apologise. It's 2665. There is reference to -- excuse me. I apologise for my confusion, but I have two exhibit numbers and neither of them seem to be correct. After -- it's 2655, after all. In this document it says that means of communication were confiscated from some international organisation, communications equipment, that is. Do you recall where these radio stations were confiscated and what the main reason was?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: This was reported to us by international NGOs on the confiscation, also on problems with the renewal of radio licences to use certain frequencies. This is what we heard and I could not -- I could not pin-point which organisation it was and which exact date. I could not.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You yourself mentioned radio frequencies. Did you get any specific information that this organisation was using MUP frequencies, although they were not authorised to do so, and that that was the reason for the confiscation of the communications equipment?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: No, I haven't heard of that. I just heard that from policemen that they were communicating by radio with UCK at times, but anything else on usage of police frequencies, I never heard anything about.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you ever hear on some other occasion that the communications equipment was confiscated from other international organisations?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: I believe KVM had their communications equipment. We used satellite phones to communicate out in the field as -- also as a security measure for us because cellphones did not work. But it was only the bigger international organisations like UNHCR, ICRC, and maybe some NGOs, bigger NGOs, international NGOs who used radio communication.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You never heard that such equipment was confiscated from somebody else?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: No, not that I can recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. There's also reference to a leaflet calling on citizens to return, but in the report it says that this was not a good method to get people to return home. Do you mean that it was insufficient or not good enough or do you think that it was a mistake to call people -- to call up on people to return?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: Well, if people have fled the area because they fear MUP and then MUP sends leaflets or drops leaflets and says, "It's safe to return," I don't think it's a convincing method to get these people back. That's why we made our efforts to have international observers there to give them a sense of confidence in returning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Because we have to take a break, I will put only one question now. Do you know that the KLA killed people who returned to their homes?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: The real problem was for us you had allegations and counter allegations. That's why we could only try to rely on our observers and of international organisations. We, indeed, wanted to look into issues, topics, locations where these allegations were. I mentioned before Glodjane which -- where parallel cases is an issue as well. But we wanted to make also forensic expertise on the victims of this incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm not sure that you've answered my question, though. Did you have any knowledge that the KLA killed Albanians who returned because they didn't want them to come back? They wanted to have chaos in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: JAN KICKERT
utterances.text: No, I had no such information.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Looking at the time, I think it's half past, and I wouldn't have more than 15 minutes to add to this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you have re-examination, Ms. Moeller?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: So far, Your Honours, rather not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Kickert, it's unfortunate, but we are going to have to interrupt your evidence. There's another -- we don't have the courtroom to ourselves. There's another hearing at 4.00 and it takes half an hour to arrange for the transfer between one case and another. So even though your time here tomorrow will apparently be brief, I'm afraid we're stuck with that situation. So I have to simply remind you of the obligation not to discuss your evidence with anybody overnight and ask you to be patient and sympathetic towards us and come back here ready to resume your evidence at 9.00 tomorrow. Now, could you please leave the courtroom with the usher.
